## SI Review of the mapping twisted multilayer graphene to TBG

The alternating twist multilayer graphene (ATMG) is defined by stacking $n$ graphene layers such that the relative twist angle between layers have equal magnitude by alternating signs i.e. $\theta_{l}=(-1)^{l}\theta/2$ , $l=1,\dots,n$ . In general, this generates $n-1$ Moiré patterns which have the same wavelength but may be displaced relative to each other. We restrict ourselves to the case where such relative displacements vanish causing these Moiré patterns to align. This configuration was shown in Ref. [88] to be the energetically most stable configuration for $n=3$ and this conclusion is likely to hold for general $n$ . In the following, we will always assume the case where the Moiré patterns are all aligned.

The Hamiltonian for ATMG with $n$ layers for a single flavor (single spin-valley) is given by

$$ H({\boldsymbol{r}})=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc}-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&T({\boldsymbol{r}})&0&0&\dots\\
T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla&T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&0&\dots\\
0&T({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&T({\boldsymbol{r}})\\
0&0&T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla&\dots\\
\dots&\dots&\dots&\dots&\dots\end{array}\right) $$

where ${\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{\pm}=e^{\pm\frac{i}{4}\theta\sigma_{Z}}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}e^{\mp\frac{i}{4}\theta\sigma_{z}}$ and $T({\boldsymbol{r}})$ is given by

$$ \displaystyle T({\boldsymbol{r}})=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}w_{0}U_{0}({\boldsymbol{r}})&w_{1}U_{1}({\boldsymbol{r}})\\
w_{1}U^{*}_{1}(-{\boldsymbol{r}})&w_{0}U_{0}({\boldsymbol{r}})\end{array}\right),\qquad U_{m}({\boldsymbol{r}})=\sum_{n=1}^{3}e^{\frac{2\pi i}{3}m(n-1)}e^{-i{\boldsymbol{q}}_{n}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}, \displaystyle{\boldsymbol{q}}_{n}=2k_{D}\sin\left(\frac{\theta}{2}\right)R_{\frac{2\pi(n-1)}{3}}(0,-1) $$

where $R_{\phi}$ denotes counter clockwise rotation by $\phi$ and $k_{D}=\frac{4\pi}{3\sqrt{3}a_{\rm CC}}$ . We would also like to consider the effect of vertical displacement field and in-plane magnetic field given by

$$ H^{U}_{l,l^{\prime}}=U\delta_{l,l^{\prime}}\left[\frac{l-1}{n-1}-\frac{1}{2}\right],\qquad H^{B}_{l,l^{\prime}}=g_{\text{orb}}\mu_{B}\delta_{l,l^{\prime}}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{(-1)^{l-1}}\cdot(\hat{z}\times{\bf B}_{\parallel})\left[l-1-\frac{n-1}{2}\right] $$

In the following, we will ignore the small $\theta$ rotation where $g_{\text{orb}}=\frac{ev_{F}d}{\mu_{B}}$ where $d\approx 3.5A^{o}$ is the interlayer separation. For $v_{F}\approx 10^{6}$ m/s, $g_{\text{orb}}=6.14$ . We notice that the external fields only enter the Hamiltonian in the combinations

$$ \Gamma_{\pm}=\frac{U}{n-1}+g_{\text{orb}}\mu_{B}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{\pm}\cdot(\hat{z}\times{\bf B}_{\parallel}) $$

Note that in the limit of small angles, we can ignore the rotation in ${\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{\pm}$ and take ${\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{\pm}\approx{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}$ which leads to $\Gamma_{\pm}=\Gamma=\frac{U}{n-1}+g_{\text{orb}}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\cdot(\hat{z}\times{\bf B}_{\parallel})$ . We will however prefer to keep this rotation for the sake of generality. We can then write the effect of displacement field and in-plane magnetic field as

$$ H^{U+B}_{ll^{\prime}}=\delta_{ll^{\prime}}\Gamma_{(-1)^{l-1}}\left[l-1-\frac{n-1}{2}\right]. $$

A remarkable result proved in Ref. [72] is that the Hamiltonian (S1) maps to $m$ copies of TBG with rescaled tunneling matrices $T$ for $n=2m$ and to $m$ copies of TBG (also with rescaled tunneling matrices $T$ ) in addition to a single Dirac cone for $n=2m+1$ . To understand this mapping, we follow Ref. [72] and perform the transformation $\tilde{H}=P^{T}HP$ with $P$ defined as

$$ P=\sum_{k=1}^{n_{e}}\delta_{2k,n_{o}+k}+\sum_{k=1}^{n_{o}}\delta_{2k-1,k} $$

where $n_{e/o}$ simply denote the number of layers with even/odd index (assuming layers are number from 1 to $n$ ) which are given by

$$ n_{e}=\lfloor n/2\rfloor,\qquad n_{o}=\lceil n/2\rceil $$

This transformation simply relabels the layers such that the Hamiltonian has a block matrix structure in the even-odd layer index

$$ \tilde{H}=P^{T}HP=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&T({\boldsymbol{r}})\otimes W\\
T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})\otimes W^{\dagger}&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla\end{array}\right), $$

with $W$ being an $n_{o}\times n_{e}$ describing the structure of the tunneling between layers. Since tunneling only takes place between nearest neighboring layers, $W$ has the simple form $W_{ij}=\delta_{i,j}+\delta_{i,j+1}$ . The mapping can be established by writing the singular value decomposition for $W=A\Lambda B^{T}$ which implies that

$$ H^{\prime}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}A^{T}&0\\
0&B^{T}\end{array}\right)\tilde{H}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}A&0\\
0&B\end{array}\right)=\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&T({\boldsymbol{r}})\otimes\Lambda\\
T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})\otimes\Lambda^{\dagger}&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla\end{array}\right) $$

Here, $\Lambda$ is an $n_{o}\times n_{e}$ matrix with non-vanishing entries only along the diagonal which we denote by $\lambda_{k}$ where $k=1,\dots,n_{e}$ . For even $n$ , $n_{e}=n_{o}=n/2$ and this mapping means that the Hamiltonian $H^{\prime}$ decomposes into a sum of $n/2$ TBG Hamiltonians with the tunneling $T({\boldsymbol{r}})$ rescaled by $\lambda_{k}$ :

$$ H^{\rm even}_{\rm dec}=PH^{\prime}_{\rm even}P^{T}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc}-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&\lambda_{1}T({\boldsymbol{r}})&0&0&\dots\\
\lambda_{1}T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla&0&0&\dots\\
0&0&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&\lambda_{2}T({\boldsymbol{r}})&\dots\\
0&0&\lambda_{2}T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla&\dots\\
\dots&\dots&\dots&\dots&\dots\end{array}\right) $$

For odd $n$ , the Hamiltonian $H^{\prime}$ reduces to $(n-1)/2$ TBG Hamiltonians with the tunneling $T({\boldsymbol{r}})$ rescaled by $\lambda_{k}$ in addition to a single Dirac cone that is decoupled from the rest of the system:

$$ H^{\rm odd}_{\rm dec}=PH^{\prime}_{\rm odd}P^{T}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccccc}-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&\lambda_{1}T({\boldsymbol{r}})&0&0&\dots&\dots\\
\lambda_{1}T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla&0&0&\dots&\dots\\
0&0&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&\lambda_{2}T({\boldsymbol{r}})&\dots&\dots\\
0&0&\lambda_{2}T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla&\dots&\dots\\
\dots&\dots&\dots&\dots&\dots&\dots\\
\dots&\dots&\dots&\dots&\dots&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla\end{array}\right) $$

The general unitary matrix which maps $H$ to a decoupled sum of TBGs possibly in addition to a Dirac cone has the explicit form

$$ V=P\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}A&0\\
0&B\end{array}\right)P^{T},\quad\implies\quad H_{\rm dec}=V^{T}HV $$

The eigenvalues $\lambda_{k}$ as well as the matrices $A$ and $B$ can be obtained by finding the eigenvalues and eigenvectors of $W^{T}W$ and $WW^{T}$

$$ \displaystyle W^{T}Wu_{k}=\lambda_{k}u_{k},\qquad k=1,\dots,n_{e} \displaystyle WW^{T}v_{k}=\lambda_{k}v_{k}\qquad k=1,\dots,n_{o} $$

It is straightforward to verify that

$$ \displaystyle\lambda_{k}=2\cos\frac{\pi k}{n+1}, \displaystyle u_{k,m}=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{n+1}m(2k-\delta_{n\,{\rm mod}\,2,0})\right),\qquad m=1,\dots,n_{e} \displaystyle v_{k,m}=\sin\left(\frac{\pi}{n+1}k(2m-\delta_{n\,{\rm mod}\,2,1})\right)\qquad m=1,\dots,n_{o} $$

The normalization of the wavefunctions is given by

$$ \beta_{k}=\left(\sum_{m=1}^{n_{e}}|u_{k,m}|^{2}\right)^{-1/2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{n+1}},\qquad\chi_{k}=\left(\sum_{m=1}^{n_{o}}|v_{k,m}|^{2}\right)^{-1/2}=\frac{2}{\sqrt{n+1}}\begin{cases}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}&:k=n_{e}+1\\
1&:\text{otherwise}\end{cases} $$

This leads to the explicit expressions for $A$ and $B$ as

$$ A_{km}=\chi_{k}v_{k,m},\qquad B_{km}=\beta_{k}u_{k,m} $$

The effect of vertical displacement field and in-plane magnetic field in the decoupled picture can be simply obtained via

$$ H^{U+B}_{\rm dec}=V^{T}H^{U+B}V $$

In the following, let us consider some explicit cases.

### SI.1 Trilayer $n=3$

The simplest example of ATMG corresponds to the trilayer case with $n=3$ . The Hamiltonian for this case is given explicitly by

$$ H({\boldsymbol{r}})=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&T({\boldsymbol{r}})&0\\
T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla&T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})\\
0&T({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla\end{array}\right) $$

The decoupling matrix $V$ can be obtained easily following the general procedure explains above. Its explicit form is given by

$$ V=P\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}A&0\\
0&B\end{array}\right)P^{T}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}&0&-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\\
0&1&0\\
\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}&0&\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}\end{array}\right) $$

The full Hamiltonian in the decoupled basis has the form

$$ H^{\rm Full}_{\rm dec}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&\sqrt{2}T({\boldsymbol{r}})&\Gamma_{+}\\
\sqrt{2}T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla&0\\
\Gamma_{+}&0&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla\end{array}\right) $$

We see that the Hamiltonian maps to a direct sum of a TBG Hamiltonian with the interlayer tunneling scaled by $\sqrt{2}$ and a single Dirac cone. The two are coupled through the displacement field $U$ and the in-plane field ${\bf B}$ .

### SI.2 Tetralayer $n=4$

We can similarly work out the Hamiltonian for the tetralayer case $n=4$ . The Hamiltonian for this case is given explicitly by

$$ H({\boldsymbol{r}})=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&T({\boldsymbol{r}})&0&0\\
T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla&T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&0\\
0&T({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&T({\boldsymbol{r}})\\
0&0&T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla\end{array}\right) $$

The decoupling matrix $V$ is

$$ V=\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}\sin\frac{\pi}{5}&0&-\sin\frac{2\pi}{5}&0\\
0&\sin\frac{2\pi}{5}&0&-\sin\frac{\pi}{5}\\
\sin\frac{2\pi}{5}&0&\sin\frac{\pi}{5}&0\\
0&\sin\frac{\pi}{5}&0&\sin\frac{2\pi}{5}\end{array}\right) $$

leading to the Hamiltonian

$$ H^{\rm Full}_{\rm dec}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla-r_{1}\Gamma_{+}&\varphi T({\boldsymbol{r}})&\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\Gamma_{+}&0\\
\varphi T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla+r_{1}\Gamma_{-}&0&\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\Gamma_{-}\\
\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\Gamma_{+}&0&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla-r_{2}\Gamma_{+}&\frac{1}{\varphi}T({\boldsymbol{r}})\\
0&\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\Gamma_{-}&\frac{1}{\varphi}T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla+r_{2}\Gamma_{-}\end{array}\right) $$

where $\varphi$ is the golden ratio $\frac{1+\sqrt{5}}{2}$ and $r_{1,2}=\frac{2\sqrt{5}\mp 5}{10}$ . Thus, the tetralayer system maps to a pair of TBGs whose interlayer tunneling is scaled by $\varphi$ and $1/\varphi$ . This yields two sequences of magic angles obtained from TBG magic angles either by multiplying or dividing by the golden ratio $\varphi$ [72]. This mapping can also be understood in terms of bonding and antibonding orbitals as follows. The first TBG (with $T$ rescaled by $\varphi$ ) is built using the bonding orbitals between the first and third (layer 1) and second and fourth (layer 2) whereas the second TBG (with $T$ rescaled by $1/\varphi$ ) is built using the antibonding orbitals between the first and third (as layer 1) and second and fourth (as layer 2). Including vertical displacement field and/or in-plane magnetic field leads to a coupling between the two TBGs. In addition, it also introduces an effective displacement field and in-plane magnetic field in each of the two TBGs that are rescaled by $\frac{1}{3}r_{1,2}$ and $r_{1,2}$ , respectively, relative to the corresponding fields applied for the four layer system.

We notice that the scaling ratio for the external fields relevant to the first TBG block is very small $r_{1}\approx-0.05$ . This smallness can be explained by explicitly computing the parameter $r_{k}$ for $n=2p$ which is given by

$$ \displaystyle r_{k}=-\frac{4}{2p+1}\sum_{m=1}^{p}(2m-1/2-p)\sin^{2}\frac{2\pi km}{2p+1}=-\frac{3+\cos\frac{4k\pi}{2p+1}-4\cos\frac{4k\pi(p+1)}{(2p+1)}}{4(2p+1)\sin^{2}\frac{2\pi k}{2p+1}}\approx-\frac{\pi^{2}k^{2}}{16p^{3}}+O(p^{-4}) $$

For $k\ll p$ and $p\gg 1$ , this implies that $r_{k}$ is very small. In particular, this means that $r_{1}$ , relevant for the first TBG block where the first magic angle is realized, is always small for any even number of layers $n=2p$ with $p>1$ due to the very rapid decrease of $r_{1}$ with $p$ .

### SI.3 $n=5$

Finally, let us consider the case $n=5$ . The Hamiltonian for this case is given explicitly by

$$ H({\boldsymbol{r}})=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc}-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&T({\boldsymbol{r}})&0&0&0\\
T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla&T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&0&0\\
0&T({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&T({\boldsymbol{r}})&0\\
0&0&T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla&T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})\\
0&0&0&T({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla\end{array}\right) $$

The decoupling matrix $V$ is

$$ V=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc}\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}&0&-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}&0&\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\
0&\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}&0&-\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}&0\\
\frac{\sqrt{2}}{\sqrt{3}}&0&0&0&-\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\\
0&\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}&0&\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}&0\\
\frac{1}{\sqrt{6}}&0&\frac{1}{\sqrt{2}}&0&\frac{1}{\sqrt{3}}\end{array}\right) $$

leading to the Hamiltonian

$$ H^{\rm Full}_{\rm dec}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc}-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&\sqrt{3}T({\boldsymbol{r}})&\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\Gamma_{+}&0&0\\
\sqrt{3}T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla&0&\Gamma_{-}&0\\
\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\Gamma_{+}&0&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&T({\boldsymbol{r}})&\frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\Gamma_{+}\\
0&\Gamma_{-}&T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla&0\\
0&0&\frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\Gamma_{+}&0&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla\end{array}\right) $$

Note that here, similar to the trilayer case, the displacement and in-plane fields only introduce a coupling between the different TBG/Dirac sectors without introducing an effective displacement field or magnetic field in each sector.

## SII Lattice relaxation

### SII.1 Summary of relaxation calculation

Here, we provide details of the lattice relaxation model. We employ a continuum model based on local configuration to obtain the relaxation pattern of the multi-layered heterostructures [90]. Every real space position $\boldsymbol{r}$ can be uniquely parametrized by a local shift vector $\boldsymbol{b}$ that describes its local environment with respect to its neighboring layers. Letting $A_{1}$ , $A_{2}$ be the matrices whose columns are the lattice vectors of layers 1 and 2 respectively and defining $A_{\delta 1}=I-A_{1}A_{2}^{-1}$ and $A_{\delta 2}=I-A_{2}A_{1}^{-1}$ , the local configuration vectors are given as $\boldsymbol{b}^{(\ell)}=A_{\delta\ell}\boldsymbol{r}$ for $\ell=1,2$ . Note that $\boldsymbol{b}^{(1)}=-\boldsymbol{b}^{(2)}$ , and only $\boldsymbol{b}^{(1)}$ and $\boldsymbol{b}^{(2)}$ are needed because there is only a single twist angle and every other layer is aligned. The relaxation vectors $\boldsymbol{u}^{(\ell)}$ have a symmetry dictated by the symmetry of the system depending on whether the number of layer $n$ is even or odd. If $n=2k$ , where $k\in\mathbb{Z}$ , $\boldsymbol{u}^{(\ell)}=-\boldsymbol{u}^{(n+1-\ell)}$ . If $n=2k+1$ , $\boldsymbol{u}^{(\ell)}=\boldsymbol{u}^{(n+1-\ell)}$ $\forall\ell\neq\frac{n+1}{2}$ .

We minimize the total energy as a function of the relaxation displacement vectors in local configuration space, and the total energy is consisted of intralayer and interlayer terms. The intralayer term can be obtained from linear elasticity theory:

$$ \displaystyle E^{\mathrm{intra}}(\boldsymbol{u}^{(\ell)})=\sum_{\ell=1}^{n}\int\frac{G}{2}(\partial_{x}u^{(\ell)}_{x}+\partial_{y}u^{(\ell)}_{y})^{2}+\frac{K}{2}\left\{(\partial_{x}u^{(\ell)}_{x}-\partial_{y}u^{(\ell)}_{y})^{2}+(\partial_{x}u^{(\ell)}_{y}+\partial_{y}u^{(\ell)}_{x})^{2}\right\}d^{2}\boldsymbol{b}, $$

where $G$ and $K$ are shear and bulk modulus of a monolayer graphene, which we take to be $G=47352\,\mathrm{meV/unit\ cell}$ , $K=69518\,\mathrm{meV/unit\ cell}$ [90].

The interlayer energy accounts for the energy cost of the layer misalignment, which is described by generalized stacking fault energy (GSFE) [104], obtained using first principles Density Functional Theory (DFT) with the Vienna Ab initio Simulation Package (VASP) [111, 112]. The GSFE is the total energy of an untwisted bilayer per unit cell as a function of the local stacking between the adjacent layers, and with the lowest energy stacking identified as zero energy. For bilayer graphene, the GSFE is maximized at the AA stacking and minimized at the AB/BA stacking. Letting $\boldsymbol{b}=(b_{x},b_{y})$ be the relative stacking between two layers, we define the following unitless vector $\boldsymbol{v}=(v,w)\in[0,2\pi]^{2}$ to describe all possible configurations:

$$ \begin{pmatrix}v\\
w\end{pmatrix}=\frac{2\pi}{a_{0}}\matrixquantity[\lx@physics@matrix\sqrt{3}/2 & -1/2 \\ \sqrt{3}/2 & 1/2\endlx@physics@matrix]\begin{pmatrix}b_{x}\\
b_{y}\end{pmatrix}, $$

where $a_{0}=2.4595$ Åis the graphene lattice constant. We then parametrize the GSFE as follows,

$$ \displaystyle V^{\mathrm{GSFE}}=c_{0}+ \displaystyle c_{1}(\cos v+\cos w+\cos(v + w)) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle c_{2}(\cos(v + 2w)+\cos(v-w)+\cos(2 v + w)) \displaystyle+ \displaystyle c_{3}(\cos(2 v )+\cos(2 w)+\cos(2 v + 2 w)), $$

where we take $c_{0}=6.832\,\mathrm{meV/cell}$ , $c_{1}=4.064\,\mathrm{meV/cell}$ , $c_{2}=-0.374\,\mathrm{meV/cell}$ , $c_{3}=-0.0095\,\mathrm{meV/cell}$ [90]. These energies were derived from DFT calculations with a van der Waals force implemented through the vdW-DFT method and the SCAN+rVV10 functional [113, 114, 115, 116]. In terms of $V^{\mathrm{GSFE}}$ , the total interlayer energy can be expressed as follows:

$$ \displaystyle E^{\mathrm{inter}}(\boldsymbol{u}^{(\ell)}) \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\ell=1}^{n-1}\int V^{\mathrm{GSFE}}(\boldsymbol{B}^{\ell\rightarrow\ell+1})\,d^{2}\boldsymbol{b}, $$

where $\boldsymbol{B}^{\ell\rightarrow\ell+1}=\boldsymbol{b}^{(\ell+1)}+{\boldsymbol{u}}^{(\ell+1)}-{\boldsymbol{u}}^{(\ell)}$ is the relaxation modified local shift vector. Note that we only consider the interaction energy between adjacent pairs of layers. The total energy is obtained by summing over uniformly sampled configuration space, justified by the ergodicity of incommensurate lattices [117, 118].

Figure S1 shows the magnitude of relaxation as a function of $\theta$ for $n=2,3,4,5$ . For a generic $n>2$ , the relaxation magnitude has two asymptotic values, depending on the number of neighboring layers. For example, when $n=3$ , layers 1 and 3 have only one adjacent layer, and layer 2 is sandwiched between the top and bottom layers. As a result, when $\theta\gtrsim 1^{\circ}$ , layers 1 and 2 have the same magnitude as that of the bilayer graphene, and layer 2 has roughly doubled magnitude due to the doubled interlayer interaction. This can be generalized to an arbitrary $n>2$ – the relaxation magnitude of the middle layers is twice as that of the top and bottom layers. The magnitude at a smaller angle depends on the number of layers, but for the magic angles considered in this work ( $\theta>1^{\circ}$ ), this effect is negligible.

$$ H({\boldsymbol{r}})=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc}-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&T_{12}({\boldsymbol{r}})&0&0&\dots\\

0&T_{32}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&T_{34}({\boldsymbol{r}})\\

To define the magic angle in this case we go to the chiral limit by setting $w_{0}^{ij}$ to zero; away from the chiral limit, there is no unique way to define the magic angle [29], so we always define the magic angle to be the one at the chiral limit. We can follow the same steps as before using the matrix $P$ from Eq. S8 to write the Hamiltonian in the even-odd layer basis as

$$ T({\boldsymbol{r}})=w_{1}\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&U_{1}({\boldsymbol{r}})\\

\dots&\dots&\dots&\dots\end{array}\right) $$

where $w_{1}\approx 110$ meV is the relaxation-independent value which we introduced to ensure notational consistency with the case of equal interlayer coupling considered earlier. As in the uniform case, we can introduce the singular value decomposition of $W$ and use it to map the multilayer Hamiltonian to a set of decoupled TBG Hamiltonians (plus a graphene Hamiltonian for $n$ odd). Denoting the eigenvalues of $W(\theta)$ by $\lambda_{k}(\theta)$ as before, we can write the magic angles for the decoupled TBG as

$$ \frac{\theta}{\lambda_{k}(\theta)}=\theta^{\rm TBG}_{\rm magic} $$

where $\theta^{\rm TBG}_{\rm magic}$ is the TBG magic angle. Due to the $\theta$ dependence of $\lambda_{k}$ , this equation can only be solved numerically leading to the value in Table 1 in the main text. All magic angles of interest (first magic angle for $n=3,4$ and second magic angle for $n=5$ ) follow from taking $\theta^{\rm TBG}_{\rm magic}$ to be the first magic angle of TBG which is equal to 1.06o assuming the $\theta$ -independent value $w_{1}=110$ meV.
