## SIII Intra-TBG effects of external fields

For an even number of layers, there is no $M_{z}$ symmetry and so the electric and magnetic fields act within the TBG sectors, not only as tunnelings between them. To understand the intra-TBG effects of the external fields in perturbation theory it is sufficient to consider $n=2$ MATBG and then straightforwardly generalize the results to $n>2$ even.

### SIII.1 External fields in $n=2$ MATBG

We begin with the unperturbed interacting Hamiltonian after integrating out remote MATBG bands

$$ \displaystyle\mathcal{H} \displaystyle=\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\rm eff}({\boldsymbol{q}})\delta\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}\delta\rho_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}},\qquad\delta\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}=\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}-\overline{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{q}} \displaystyle\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}} \displaystyle=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})c_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}},\qquad\overline{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{q}}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{G}},{\boldsymbol{k}}}\delta_{{\boldsymbol{G}},{\boldsymbol{q}}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}({\boldsymbol{k}}), $$

where, in this section, $\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ is chirally symmetric form factor for MATBG [30]:

$$ \Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\Lambda^{S}_{c{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}})=F_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})e^{i\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\gamma_{z}}. $$

and $C_{2}$ symmetry implies that

$$ F_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}(-{\boldsymbol{k}})=F_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\qquad\phi_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}(-{\boldsymbol{k}})=\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}}). $$

In other subsections we will use the subscript $c$ to clarify that it refers to the form factors of the magic sector. The superscript $S$ which we will usually omit differentiates this symmetric part of the form factor from the much smaller chirally-asymmetric part $\Lambda^{A}_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})=-\gamma_{z}\Lambda^{A}_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\gamma_{z}$ . The presence of $\Lambda^{A}$ gives rise to the anisotropy $\lambda=\frac{A_{M}}{2A^{2}}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}{\boldsymbol{k}}}V({\boldsymbol{q}})\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})^{2}$ , whereas the chern off-diagonal dispersion $h_{c}$ gives the superexchange $J\propto h^{2}/U$ [31].

The Hamiltonian (S52) has a manifold of quantum Hall ferromagnetic ground states with a ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent $Q$ matrix with definite Chern number: $[Q,\gamma_{z}]=0$ . It also has a ${\rm U}(2n)\times{\rm U}(2n)$ symmetry, where $n$ is the number of spin components, consisting of arbitrary unitary rotations in each Chern sector. For large $\kappa$ the model (S52) has an approximate ${\rm U}(4n)$ symmetry due to concentration of Berry curvature [32]; this emergent symmetry will be important when we consider MSM states at the end of this section. We briefly review this now. Consider the limit where the Berry curvature is perfectly solenoidal at the $\Gamma$ point such that the Berry connection ${\boldsymbol{A}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\gamma_{z}(-k_{y},k_{x})/\absolutevalue{\bk}^{2}$ . Then the Berry connection vanishes after the singular gauge transformation

$$ c_{\boldsymbol{k}}\to e^{i\theta_{\boldsymbol{k}}\gamma_{z}}c_{\boldsymbol{k}},\qquad\theta_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\arg(k_{x}+ik_{y}). $$

After this transformation all $4n$ Chern bands have the form factor $\Lambda^{\prime}_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\approx F_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ and may be rotated into each other. Ground states consist of ${\rm U}(4n)$ ferromagnets with $Q^{\prime}=e^{i\theta_{\boldsymbol{k}}\gamma_{z}}Qe^{-i\theta_{\boldsymbol{k}}\gamma_{z}}$ . This transformation does nothing to Chern diagonal states but turns nematic semimetals into quantum Hall ferromagnets with $Q^{\prime}\propto\gamma_{x,y}$ and ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent.

We will use the hatted notation for second quantized operators above for the rest of this section, together with the following identities for expectation values [31]:

$$ \hat{A}=\sum_{\alpha\beta}c^{\dagger}_{\alpha}A_{\alpha\beta}c_{\beta},\qquad\langle\hat{A}\rangle=\Tr\tilde{P}A,\qquad\langle\hat{A}\hat{B}\rangle=\Tr\tilde{P}AB-\Tr A\tilde{P}B\tilde{P}+\Tr\tilde{P}A\Tr\tilde{P}B, $$

The upper case trace denotes a sum over momentum and orbital indices whereas a lower case trace denotes a sum over orbital indices only. This notation is useful in part because “hatting” preserves commutators:

$$ [c^{\dagger}_{\alpha}c_{\beta},c^{\dagger}_{\gamma}c_{\delta}]=\delta_{\beta\gamma}c^{\dagger}_{\alpha}c_{\delta}-\delta_{\alpha\delta}c^{\dagger}_{\gamma}c_{\beta}\quad\implies\quad[\hat{A},\hat{B}]=\widehat{[A,B]} $$

In this notation, the density operator is

$$ \rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}=\hat{\Lambda}_{\boldsymbol{q}},\qquad(\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}})_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}=\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\delta_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}. $$

We project external field terms

$$ \frac{1}{2}\left(V+g_{\text{orb}}\mu_{B}(\hat{{\boldsymbol{z}}}\times{\bf B})\cdot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\right)\mu_{z}, $$

to the Chern/valley flat band basis. The operator $\mu_{z}=\pm$ labels the two TBG layers. The electric field term is diagonal in Chern sector and valley. It is symmetric under $C_{2}\mathcal{T}$ and is therefore proportional to $\gamma_{0}$ after projection. The factor of $\mu_{z}$ means that it is odd under (unitary) $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}=i\sigma_{x}\tau_{x}\mu_{y}$ symmetry. On the flat bands $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}$ acts as $\eta_{x}\gamma_{z}$ , and so the electric field term must be proportional to $\eta_{z}$ after projection. The magnetic field is off diagonal in Chern sector and even under both $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}$ and $C_{2}\mathcal{T}$ . This fixes its form to be $\gamma_{x,y}\eta_{z}$ . After projection we obtain

$$ \displaystyle\hat{h}_{V,B} \displaystyle=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}c^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}h_{V,B}({\boldsymbol{k}})c_{\boldsymbol{k}}, \displaystyle\qquad h_{V}({\boldsymbol{k}})_{\gamma\eta\gamma^{\prime}\eta^{\prime}} \displaystyle=\bra{ u_{\bk\gamma\eta}}\frac{V}{2}\mu_{z}\ket{u_{\bk\gamma' \eta'}}=h_{0}({\boldsymbol{k}})(\eta_{z})_{\eta\eta^{\prime}}\delta_{\gamma\gamma^{\prime}}, \displaystyle\qquad h_{B}({\boldsymbol{k}})_{\gamma\eta\gamma^{\prime}\eta^{\prime}} \displaystyle=\bra{ u_{\bk\gamma\eta}}\frac{1}{2}g_{\rm orb}\mu_{B}\hat{{\boldsymbol{z}}}\times{\bf B}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}\mu_{z}\ket{u_{\bk\gamma' \eta'}}=(\eta_{z})_{\eta\eta^{\prime}}{\boldsymbol{b}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot({\boldsymbol{\gamma}})_{\gamma\gamma^{\prime}}, $$

where $h_{0}({\boldsymbol{k}})=-h_{0}(-{\boldsymbol{k}})$ by $C_{2}$ symmetry. The influence of these terms at first order is zero for Chern diagonal states: the magnetic field term is because it is off diagonal in Chern sector and $Q$ is diagonal, whereas the electric field term is odd under ${\boldsymbol{k}}\mapsto-{\boldsymbol{k}}$ and $Q$ is ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ independent. They both contribute at second order.

To obtain the second order terms we parameterize rotations outside the ground state subspace in the usual way

$$ \ket{\Psi_M}=e^{-i\hat{M}}\ket{\Psi_Q},\qquad\{M,Q\}=0. $$

For the electric field superexchange we want $[M,\gamma_{z}]=0$ whereas for the magnetic field term $\{M,\gamma_{z}\}=0$ . The interaction energy is

$$ E_{\rm int}=-\frac{1}{4A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V({\boldsymbol{q}})\langle({\rm ad}^{2}_{\hat{M}}\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}})\rho_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}+\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}{\rm ad}^{2}_{\hat{M}}\rho_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}+2{\rm ad}_{\hat{M}}\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}{\rm ad}_{\hat{M}}\rho_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rangle+\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}V({\boldsymbol{G}})\langle({\rm ad}^{2}_{\hat{M}}\rho_{\boldsymbol{G}})\overline{\rho}_{-{\boldsymbol{G}}}\rangle. $$

The first and second terms entirely cancel against the background terms because $Q$ is ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent and Chern-diagonal, and thus $[Q,\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}]=0$ . We then evaluate

$$ \displaystyle 2\langle{\rm ad}_{\hat{M}}\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}{\rm ad}_{\hat{M}}\rho_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rangle \displaystyle=2\langle\hat{[M,\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}]}\hat{[M,\Lambda_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}]}\rangle=2\Tr P[M,\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}][M,\Lambda_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}]=\Tr[M,\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}][M,\Lambda_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}] \displaystyle=-2\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(F_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}})^{2}M_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{2}-M_{\boldsymbol{k}}\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}})M_{\boldsymbol{k}}\Lambda^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\right) $$

where we used $[Q,M]=[Q,\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}]=0$ to drop the $\Tr P[M,\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}]P[M,\Lambda_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}]$ term and the $Q$ -dependent part of $\Tr P[M,\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}][M,\Lambda_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}]$ .

#### SIII.1.1 Electric field

We now specialize to the case of an electric field and handle a magnetic field after. In this case $[M_{\boldsymbol{k}},\gamma_{z}]=[M_{\boldsymbol{k}},\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})]=0$ . We separate the different Chern sectors and expand $M$ via

$$ M=\sum_{\gamma\mu}m_{\gamma\mu}r^{\mu}\gamma_{\gamma},\qquad Q=\sum_{\gamma}Q_{\gamma}\gamma_{\gamma}, $$

where $r^{\mu}$ form a basis for $2n\times 2n$ Hermitian matrices and $m_{\gamma\mu}$ are real because $M^{\dagger}=M$ . We then have

$$ E_{\rm int}=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V({\boldsymbol{q}})F_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})^{2}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(M_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{2}-M_{\boldsymbol{k}}M_{[{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}]})=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}\mu\gamma}m_{\gamma\mu{\boldsymbol{k}}}R_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}m_{\gamma\mu{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}. $$

where

$$ R_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V({\boldsymbol{q}})F_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})^{2}(\delta_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}-\delta_{[{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}],{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}), $$

and $[{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}]$ denotes the first Brillouin zone component of ${\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}$ . The first order term coupling $M$ to the displacement field is

$$ E_{V}=-i\langle[\hat{M},\hat{h}_{V}]\rangle=-\frac{i}{2}\Tr Q[M,h_{V}]=i\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}\mu\gamma}m_{\mu\gamma{\boldsymbol{k}}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}r^{\mu}Q_{\gamma}h_{V{\boldsymbol{k}}}, $$

and so we obtain the full energy

$$ E_{\rm int}+E_{V}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}\mu\gamma}m_{\gamma\mu{\boldsymbol{k}}}R_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}m_{\gamma\mu{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}+i\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}\mu\gamma}m_{\mu\gamma{\boldsymbol{k}}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Q_{\gamma}[r^{\mu},h_{V{\boldsymbol{k}}}]. $$

Minimizing with respect to $m$ then gives

$$ \displaystyle E_{\rm SE} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}\mu\gamma}\left(i\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}r^{\mu}Q_{\gamma}h_{V{\boldsymbol{k}}}\eta_{z}\right)R^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}\left(i\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}r^{\mu}Q_{\gamma}h_{V{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}\eta_{z}\right) \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}\mu\gamma}h_{V{\boldsymbol{k}}}R^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}h_{V{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}r^{\mu}\eta_{z}Q_{\gamma}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}r^{\mu}Q_{\gamma}\eta_{z}. $$

Technically, $R$ is not invertible here because it has a zero mode with $M_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ independent of ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ . This is the goldstone mode for ${\rm U}(4)\times{\rm U}(4)$ symmetry breaking. However, $h_{V}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ does not couple to this goldstone mode because it is odd under ${\boldsymbol{k}}\mapsto-{\boldsymbol{k}}$ . In practice, we may add a term $C\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(M_{\boldsymbol{k}}+M_{-{\boldsymbol{k}}})^{2}$ to the interaction energy to gap the goldstone mode but not influence the superexchange mediated by $h_{V}$ .

We now apply the Fierze identity for $r^{\mu}$ ,

$$ \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Ar^{\mu}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Br^{\mu}=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}AB-\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}QAQB\right), $$

to (S69). We have, up to an unimportant constant from the first term,

$$ E_{\rm SE}=\frac{\tilde{\lambda}_{V}}{4}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Q\eta_{z}Q\eta_{z},\qquad\tilde{\lambda}=\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}\mu\gamma}h_{V{\boldsymbol{k}}}R^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}h_{V{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}. $$

We find $\tilde{\lambda}_{V}=\frac{1}{4}c_{V}V^{2}$ , where $c_{V}$ is highly $\kappa$ dependent but always very small $c_{V}\approx 10^{-5}(\rm{meV})^{-1}$ . This is because the flat bands have almost no layer polarization, and so the electric field term projected to the flat bands is very small.

#### SIII.1.2 Magnetic field

If we instead have an in-plane magnetic field then $\{M,\gamma_{z}\}=0$ and so it may be written in a block off-diagonal form in Chern sector,

$$ M=\begin{pmatrix}0&m\\
m^{\dagger}&0\end{pmatrix}_{\gamma},\qquad m=m_{\mu}r^{\mu},\qquad r^{\mu}=-Q_{+}r^{\mu}Q_{-}. $$

The interaction energy is

$$ E_{\rm int}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}\mu\gamma}m^{*}_{\mu{\boldsymbol{k}}}R_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}m_{\gamma\mu{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}},\qquad R_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V({\boldsymbol{q}})F_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})^{2}(\delta_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}-\delta_{[{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}],{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}e^{-2i\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})}), $$

where the extra factor of $e^{-2i\phi_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})}$ arises because $M$ anticommutes with the part of the form factor that is proportional to $\gamma_{z}$ . Its presence ensures that there are no gapless inter-Chern modes.

The first order term is

$$ E_{B}=-i\langle\widehat{[M,h_{B}]}\rangle=-\frac{i}{2}\Tr Q[M,h_{B}]=-i\Tr QMh_{B}=-i\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}\mu}\left(m_{\mu}z^{*}_{b{\boldsymbol{k}}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}r^{\mu}\eta_{z}Q_{+}-m^{*}_{\mu}z_{b}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Q_{+}\eta_{z}r^{\mu{\dagger}}\right), $$

where $z_{b{\boldsymbol{k}}}=b_{x{\boldsymbol{k}}}+ib_{y{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ . Integrating out $m$ we obtain the energy

$$ E_{\rm SE}=-2\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}z^{*}_{b{\boldsymbol{k}}}R^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}z_{b{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}\sum_{\mu}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}r^{\mu}\eta_{z}Q_{+}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}r^{\mu{\dagger}}Q_{+}\eta_{z} $$

If we use the Fierz identity,

$$ \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}r^{\mu}A\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}r^{\mu{\dagger}}B=\frac{1}{2}\left(\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}AB-\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Q_{+}AQ_{-}B\right), $$

we have up to an unimportant constant

$$ E_{\rm SE}\frac{A_{M}}{A}=\frac{1}{2}\lambda_{B}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Q_{+}\eta_{z}Q_{-}\eta_{z},\qquad\lambda_{B}=\frac{2A_{M}}{A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}z^{*}_{b{\boldsymbol{k}}}R^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}z_{b{\boldsymbol{k}}}. $$

Explicitly we find $\lambda_{B}=\frac{1}{4}c_{B}g_{\text{orb}}^{2}B^{2}$ , where the coefficient $c_{B}$ increases with $\kappa$ . As $\kappa$ ranges from $0$ to $0.8$ we have $c_{B}=0.1-0.3(\rm{meV})^{-1}$ . The reason for the large coefficient $c_{B}\gg U_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{-1}$ and the strong $\kappa$ dependence is that the magnetic field couples to a nemmatic near-soft mode. The nematic soft mode becomes softer as $\kappa$ increases because the Berry curvature becomes more concentrated [32]. For this reason perturbation theory breaks down before we reach the critical field once $\kappa>0.6$ or so. Before this value of $\kappa$ we may use the above expression to predict the critical field for the KIVC $\to$ VH transition.

As discussed in the main text for large $\kappa$ it is better to think of the magnetic field as an effective “Zeeman” field for a low lying MSM state. We may model the MSM and VH states as ${\rm U}(4n)$ quantum Hall ferromagnets with $Q^{\prime}={\boldsymbol{n}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\eta_{z}$ for a three dimensional real unit vector ${\boldsymbol{n}}$ . For ${\boldsymbol{n}}$ in the $x-y$ plane we obtain a MSM state whereas for ${\boldsymbol{n}}$ along the $z$ axis we obtain a VH state. The perturbative superexchange calculation above corresponds to a small ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -dependent canting away from the VH state, whereas here we can consider a non-perturbative canting that is ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent within the manifold of ${\rm U}(4n)$ quantum Hall ferromagnets. The Zeeman energy is given by

$$ E_{B}=\frac{1}{2}\Tr Qh_{B}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left({\boldsymbol{b}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\eta_{z}e^{2i\theta_{\boldsymbol{k}}\gamma_{z}}{\boldsymbol{n}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\eta_{z}\right)=2nA{\boldsymbol{b}}^{\prime}\cdot{\boldsymbol{n}},\qquad b^{\prime}_{x}+b^{\prime}_{y}=\frac{1}{A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}e^{2i\theta_{\boldsymbol{k}}}(b_{x}+ib_{y}) $$

where ${\boldsymbol{b}}^{\prime}$ is nonzero because ${\boldsymbol{b}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ winds twice around the $\Gamma$ point. The vector ${\boldsymbol{b}}^{\prime}$ may be thought of as the projection of the magnetic field ${\bf B}$ onto the space of ${\rm U}(4n)$ -related ground states; it rotates once when the magnetic field does as one would expect. This is the Zeeman energy we use to predict the transitions in the main text for large $\kappa$ .

### SIII.2 Even n¿2

We now discuss the effects of the external fields for even $n>2$ . For odd $n$ there is no such external field contribution because the external fields only connect opposite $M_{z}$ sectors. We again assume that one TBG is magic and the other TBGs are weakly coupled. As for the odd $n$ case there are superexchange terms arising from field-induced tunneling between different TBGs. However, the most important effect for the magic $n=2$ TBG is the intra-TBG superexchange. This may be computed in the same way as for $n=2$ , but with a coefficient that depends on how the external fields couple to the TBG in question.

For example, consider $n=4$ with the BM Hamiltonian copied here for convenience,

$$ H^{\rm Full}_{\rm dec}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla-r_{1}\Gamma_{+}&\varphi T({\boldsymbol{r}})&\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\Gamma_{+}&0\\
\varphi T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla+r_{1}\Gamma_{-}&0&\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\Gamma_{-}\\
\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\Gamma_{+}&0&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla-r_{2}\Gamma_{+}&\frac{1}{\varphi}T({\boldsymbol{r}})\\
0&\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\Gamma_{-}&\frac{1}{\varphi}T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla+r_{2}\Gamma_{-}\end{array}\right). $$

The strength of the intra-TBG superexchange is proportional to the couplings $r_{1,2}=\frac{2\sqrt{5}\mp 5}{10}$ . It is important to note that $r_{1}\approx 1/20$ , and therefore critical fields could be as much as ten times larger for four-layer graphene for this TBG subsystem compared to $n=2$ TBG. As discussed in SI, this is generic for $n>2$ even; we have $r_{1}\approx\frac{\pi^{2}}{2n^{3}}$ .

## SIV Field mediated superexchange for $n>2$

In this section we compute the energy associated with superexchange between TBG or graphene sectors mediated by the displacement field. We follow a very similar methodology to [31] where the $J$ and $\lambda$ terms in (20) were calculated, but the discussion here will be self contained. We focus on the $n=3$ trilayer case first and then describe the modifications associated with TBG-TBG superexchange in four and higher layers.

### SIV.1 n=3 MATTG mirror superexchange

For $n=3$ we start with the Hamiltonian

$$ \begin{aligned} \mathcal{H}_{\rm eff}&=\mathcal{H}_{D}+\mathcal{H}_{\rm int}\\
\mathcal{H}_{\rm D}&=\sum_{{\bf p}}\sum_{\eta}f_{{\bf p}}^{\dagger}\left(v\eta{\bf p}_{\eta}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}-\mu\right)f_{{\bf p}},\\
\mathcal{H}_{\rm int}&=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\rm eff}({\boldsymbol{q}})\delta\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}\delta\rho_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}},\\
\delta\rho&=\delta\rho^{S}+\delta\rho_{f}\end{aligned}, $$

where ${\bf p}_{\eta}={\bf p}-{\boldsymbol{K}}_{\eta}$ and ${\bf p}={\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}}$ where ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ is restricted to the first Brillouin zone. While the TBG flat bands are natural to describe in the first moiré Brillouin zone, we will opt to label the graphene electrons with an unfolded ${\bf p}$ . The density operator and form factor break into TBG and graphene parts:

$$ \rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}=\hat{\tilde{\Lambda}}_{\boldsymbol{q}},\qquad(\tilde{\Lambda}_{\boldsymbol{q}})_{{\boldsymbol{k}}{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}=\tilde{\Lambda}_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\delta_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}},\qquad\tilde{\Lambda}_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})=\begin{pmatrix}\Lambda_{c{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}})&0\\
0&\Lambda_{f{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\end{pmatrix}. $$

The mean field ground state of this Hamiltonian is a Slater determinant state specified by

$$ \tilde{P}=\begin{pmatrix}P_{c}&0\\
0&P_{f}\end{pmatrix}=\frac{1}{2}(1+\tilde{Q}),\qquad\tilde{Q}=\begin{pmatrix}Q_{c}&0\\
0&Q_{f}\end{pmatrix},\qquad P_{c\alpha\beta}=\langle c^{\dagger}_{\beta}c_{\alpha}\rangle\qquad P_{f\alpha\beta}=\langle f^{\dagger}_{\beta}f_{\alpha}\rangle, $$

where $Q_{c}$ is ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent, at least approximately near the ${\boldsymbol{K}}_{\eta}$ points where the superexchange is active, and

$$ Q_{f}({\bf p})=\sum_{\eta=\pm}Q_{f\eta}({\bf p})\eta_{\eta},\qquad Q_{f\eta}({\bf p})=-\eta\frac{{\bf p}_{\eta}}{\absolutevalue{\bp_\eta}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\Theta(v\absolutevalue{\bp_\eta}-\absolutevalue{\mu})+\mathop{\mathrm{sgn}}{\mu}\,\Theta(\absolutevalue{\mu}-v\absolutevalue{\bp_\eta}) $$

describes occupation of graphene electrons. We used the notation

$$ \eta_{\pm}=\frac{1}{2}(1\pm\eta_{z})\qquad\gamma_{\pm}=\frac{1}{2}(1\pm\gamma_{z}). $$

It is important to note that small graphene masses and dopings are arbitrarily low energy excited states and may be favored by small displacement fields or in plane magnetic fields, depending on the TBG ground state. We will allow for this possibility and therefore only use (S83) in the computation of the energy gap to excited states. Similarly, we will allow the magic sector to gain a piece $\propto\gamma_{x,y}$ and therefore will only assume $Q_{c}\propto\gamma_{z}$ in the computation of the energy gap. Note that we have ignored terms proportional to $\rho^{A}$ and also the dispersion in the TBG sector. The effects of these terms are captured within perturbation theory in the $J$ and $\lambda$ terms.

We will similarly compute the order $V^{2},\,B^{2}$ terms on top of the unperturbed model (S80). The perturbations we add are the displacement field and parallel magnetic field terms (8) projected to the flat bands. In this section it will be convenient to label both the flat band and graphene electrons with the unfolded ${\bf p}$ and use a periodic gauge $c_{{\bf p}}=c_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ for the flat bands where ${\boldsymbol{k}}=[{\bf p}]$ is the first BZ part of ${\bf p}$ . We then obtain

$$ \hat{\Xi}=\sum_{{\bf p}\in\rm BZ}\tilde{c}^{\dagger}_{\bf p}\Xi_{\bf p}\tilde{c}_{\bf p}=\sum_{{\bf p}\in\rm{BZ}}c^{\dagger}_{\bf p}\xi_{\bf p}f_{\bf p}+f^{\dagger}_{\bf p}\xi^{\dagger}_{\bf p}c_{\bf p},\qquad\tilde{c}=\begin{pmatrix}c\\
f\end{pmatrix},\qquad\Xi_{\bf p}=\begin{pmatrix}0&\xi_{\bf p}\\
\xi^{\dagger}_{\bf p}&0\end{pmatrix}, $$

where $\xi_{\bf p}=v_{\bf p}+b_{\bf p}$ .

The tunnelings $\xi_{\bf p}$ are given by projecting the perturbations to the BM hamiltonian to the low energy subspace of flat bands and graphene Dirac cones. We use the complete sublattice polarization of the unperturbed TBG flat bands to only keep the Chern diagonal part of $v_{\bf p}$ and the Chern off diagonal part of $b_{\bf p}$ . We obtain

$$ \xi_{\bf p}=\sum_{\eta=\pm}\xi_{{\bf p}\eta}\eta_{\eta},\qquad(\xi_{{\bf p}\eta})_{\gamma\gamma^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{2}\left(V\delta_{\gamma\gamma^{\prime}}+\eta{\boldsymbol{A}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}_{\gamma\gamma^{\prime}}\right)t_{{\bf p}\eta\gamma} $$

with no implied summation over $\eta$ or $\gamma$ . The spatial wavefunction overlap is

$$ t_{{\bf p}\eta\gamma}=\int_{\rm Cell}d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}\,u^{*}_{+{\bf p}\eta\gamma+}({\boldsymbol{r}})=\int_{\rm Cell}d^{2}{\boldsymbol{r}}u^{*}_{+{\boldsymbol{k}}\eta\gamma+}({\boldsymbol{r}})e^{i{\boldsymbol{G}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{r}}}, $$

where $u_{+{\bf p}\eta\gamma\mu}({\boldsymbol{r}})$ is mirror $+1$ moiré periodic wavefunction in graphene valley $\eta$ and Chern sector $\gamma$ evaluated in TBG “layer” $\mu$ and position ${\boldsymbol{r}}$ . As before ${\bf p}={\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}}$ .

The operator $\hat{\Xi}$ is zero in the ground state subspace of $Q$ matrices that are mirror diagonal. Its contribution comes from superexchange at second order. Application of $\hat{\Xi}$ generates rotations outside of the ground state manifold; these excited states may be paramterized as

$$ \ket{\Psi_M}=e^{-i\hat{M}}\ket{\Psi_{\tilde{Q}}},\qquad\{M,M_{z}\}=\{M,\tilde{Q}\}=0. $$

We will calculate the expectation value of the Hamiltonian in the state $\ket{\Psi_M}$ up to second order in $M$ . We will then integrate out $M$ to obtain the superexchange contribution to the energy functional.

First it is convenient to find a simple parameterization of $M$ . The anticommutation with $M_{z}$ and $\tilde{Q}$ imply that we can write $M$ as

$$ M=\begin{pmatrix}0&m\\
m^{\dagger}&0\end{pmatrix}\qquad Q_{c}mQ_{f}=-m. $$

We also flip momenta in one valley within the graphene sector so that the location of the graphene Dirac point in both valleys can be the same; this recovers some of the pseudospin isotropy. This is carried out by the change of variables

$$ m_{\bf p}=w_{1{\bf p}}\eta_{+}+w_{2-{\bf p}}\eta_{-}+w_{3{\bf p}}\eta_{x}\eta_{+}+w_{4-{\bf p}}\eta_{x}\eta_{-},\qquad w_{\bf p}=w_{1{\bf p}}\eta_{+}+w_{2{\bf p}}\eta_{-}+w_{3{\bf p}}\eta_{x}\eta_{+}+w_{4{\bf p}}\eta_{x}\eta_{-}. $$

such that $Q_{c}wQ^{\prime}_{f}=-w$ where

$$ Q^{\prime}_{f}({\bf p})=Q_{f+}({\bf p})\eta_{+}+Q_{f-}(-{\bf p})\eta_{-}=-\frac{{\bf p}_{+}}{\absolutevalue{\bp_+}}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}\Theta(v\absolutevalue{\bp_+}-\absolutevalue{\mu})+\mathop{\mathrm{sgn}}{\mu}\,\Theta(\absolutevalue{\mu}-v\absolutevalue{\bp_+}) $$

is now the identity in pseudospin space.

Finally, for the purpose of eventually integrating out $w$ , we expand

$$ w_{\bf p}=\sum_{\mu\nu}C^{\mu\nu}_{\bf p}w_{{\bf p}\nu}t_{\mu}\qquad t_{\mu}C^{\mu\nu}_{\bf p}=\frac{1}{2}\left(t_{\nu}-Q_{c}t_{\nu}Q_{f{\bf p}}^{\prime}\right) $$

where $t^{\mu}$ are a basis for $4n\times 4n$ matrices and $n$ is the number of spin components. Important cases are $n=1$ for an effective spinless model on top of a spin polarized state at $\nu=\pm 2$ and $n=2$ for $\nu=0$ . The matrix $C=C^{2}=C^{\dagger}$ projects onto the generators that are odd under $A\mapsto Q_{c}AQ^{\prime}_{f{\bf p}}$ .

We now evaluate the energy of the two terms in the Hamiltonian (S80) and that of the perturbation (S85). To evaluate expectation values we use the expansion

$$ \bra{\Psi_M}\hat{A}\ket{\Psi_M}=\langle e^{-i{\rm ad}_{\hat{M}}}A\rangle=\langle\hat{A}\rangle-i\langle{\rm ad}_{\hat{M}}A\rangle-\frac{1}{2}\langle{\rm ad}_{\hat{M}}^{2}A\rangle+\cdots $$

where ${\rm ad}_{A}B=[A,B]$ . We will use that this operation satisfies the product rule ${\rm ad}_{A}(BC)=({\rm ad}_{A}B)C+B{\rm ad}_{A}C$ . The expectation values on the right hand side are in the state $\ket{\Psi_{\tilde{Q}}}$ .

#### SIV.1.1 Graphene Dispersion

We first evaluate the graphene dispersion term. We write it as $\mathcal{H}_{D}=\sum_{\bf p}f^{\dagger}_{\bf p}h_{D}f_{\bf p}$ with $h_{D}=\sum_{\eta}\eta\eta_{\eta}v{\bf p}_{\eta}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\gamma}}-\mu$ . The zeroth order term is a constant, and the first order term vanishes by $M_{z}$ symmetry. The second order term is

$$ \displaystyle E_{D} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{2}\left\langle{\rm ad}_{\hat{M}}{\rm ad}_{\hat{M}}\begin{pmatrix}0&0\\
0&\hat{h}_{D}\end{pmatrix}\right\rangle=-\frac{1}{2}\left\langle\widehat{\left[M,\left[M,h_{D}\frac{1}{2}(1-M_{z})\right]\right]}\right\rangle=-\frac{1}{2}\Tr\tilde{P}\left[M,\left[M,h_{D}\frac{1}{2}(1-M_{z})\right]\right] \displaystyle=\Tr P_{c}mh_{D}m^{\dagger}-\frac{1}{2}\Tr P_{f}\{h_{D},m^{\dagger}m\}, $$

where in moving from the first to second line we explicitly evaluated the commutators and split the trace into separate mirror sectors. We now use $Q_{c}mQ_{f}=-m$ and its adjoint to show

$$ \Tr P_{c}mh_{D}m^{\dagger}=\frac{1}{2}\Tr P_{f}^{\perp}h_{D}m^{\dagger}m+\frac{1}{2}\Tr P_{f}^{\perp}m^{\dagger}mh_{D}, $$

where $P_{c,f}^{\perp}=\frac{1}{2}(1-Q_{c,f})$ and the two terms on the right hand side are equal. We now combine the traces in the two mirror sectors to obtain

$$ E_{D}=-\frac{1}{2}\Tr Q_{f}\{h_{D},m^{\dagger}m\}=-\frac{1}{2}\Tr\{Q_{f},h_{D}\}m^{\dagger}m $$

and with the expansion (S92),

$$ E_{D}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\bf p}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\{h^{\prime}_{D},Q^{\prime}_{f}\}w^{\dagger}_{\bf p}w_{\bf p}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\bf p}\mu}w^{*}_{{\bf p}\mu}(CR^{D}C)^{\mu\nu}_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}w_{{\bf p}\nu},\qquad R^{D\mu\nu}_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}=\delta_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\{h^{\prime}_{D},Q^{\prime}_{f}\}t_{\mu}^{\dagger}t_{\nu} $$

At charge neutrality the energy takes the simple form

$$ R^{D\mu\nu}_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}=2v\absolutevalue{\bp_+}\delta_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}\delta^{\mu\nu}. $$

#### SIV.1.2 Interaction Term

We now evaluate the interaction term. First we rewrite it using $\delta\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}=\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}-\overline{\rho}_{\boldsymbol{q}}$ :

$$ \mathcal{H}_{\rm int}=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\rm eff}({\boldsymbol{q}})\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}\rho_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}-\frac{1}{A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}V_{\rm eff}({\boldsymbol{G}})\rho_{\boldsymbol{G}}\overline{\rho}_{-{\boldsymbol{G}}}. $$

The zeroth order term is part of the constant ground state energy, independent of $M$ , and the first order term vanishes by $M_{z}$ symmetry. The second order terms are

$$ E_{\rm int}=-\frac{1}{4A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\rm eff}({\boldsymbol{q}})\langle({\rm ad}^{2}_{\hat{M}}\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}})\rho_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}+\rho_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}{\rm ad}^{2}_{\hat{M}}\rho_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}+2{\rm ad}_{\hat{M}}\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}{\rm ad}_{\hat{M}}\rho_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rangle+\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}V_{\rm eff}({\boldsymbol{G}})\langle({\rm ad}^{2}_{\hat{M}}\rho_{\boldsymbol{G}})\overline{\rho}_{-{\boldsymbol{G}}}\rangle $$

We begin with the first term

$$ \displaystyle\langle({\rm ad}^{2}_{\hat{M}}\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}})\rho_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rangle \displaystyle=\langle\widehat{[M,[M,\tilde{\Lambda}_{\boldsymbol{q}}]]}\widehat{\tilde{\Lambda}_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}}\rangle \displaystyle=\Tr\tilde{P}[M,[M,\tilde{\Lambda}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}]]\Lambda_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}-\Tr\tilde{P}[M,[M,\tilde{\Lambda}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}]]\tilde{P}\tilde{\Lambda}_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}+\Tr\tilde{P}[M,[M,\tilde{\Lambda}_{\boldsymbol{q}}]]\Tr\tilde{P}\tilde{\Lambda}_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}} \displaystyle=\Tr\tilde{P}[M,[M,\tilde{\Lambda}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}]][\tilde{\Lambda}_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}},\tilde{P}]+\sum_{{\boldsymbol{G}}}\langle[M,[M,\tilde{\Lambda}_{\boldsymbol{G}}]]\rangle\overline{\rho}_{-{\boldsymbol{G}}}\delta_{{\boldsymbol{q}},{\boldsymbol{G}}}. $$

The second term in (S101), which is only nonzero when ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ is a reciprocal lattice vector, together with the analogous contribution from the second term in (S100), cancels with the background term (final term in (S100)). We have used $\tilde{P}=\tilde{P}^{2}$ to write the first two terms in (S101) in terms of the commutator $[\tilde{\Lambda}_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}},\tilde{P}]$ which is zero in the positive mirror sector but nonzero in the negative mirror sector because $Q_{f}$ is ${\bf p}$ -dependent. An explicit expansion of the commutators yields

$$ \displaystyle\Tr\tilde{P}[M,[M,\tilde{\Lambda}_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}]][\tilde{\Lambda}_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}},\tilde{P}] \displaystyle=\Tr P_{f}\Lambda_{f{\boldsymbol{q}}}(m^{\dagger}m\Lambda_{f-{\boldsymbol{q}}}+\Lambda_{f-{\boldsymbol{q}}}m^{\dagger}m-2m^{\dagger}\Lambda_{c-{\boldsymbol{q}}})(\Lambda_{f-{\boldsymbol{q}}}P_{f}-\Lambda_{f{\boldsymbol{q}}}P_{f}) \displaystyle=\Tr(\Lambda_{f \bq} \Lambda_{f -\bq} P_f + \Lambda_{f -\bq} P_f \Lambda_{f \bq} - \Lambda_{f \bq}P_f \Lambda_{f -\bq} P_f - P_f \Lambda_{f -\bq} P_f \Lambda_{f \bq})m^{\dagger}m \displaystyle-2\Tr[\Lambda_{f-{\boldsymbol{q}}},P_{f}]P_{f}m^{\dagger}\Lambda_{c{\boldsymbol{q}}}m, $$

and the analogous contribution from $\langle\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}{\rm ad}_{\hat{M}}^{2}\rho_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rangle$ is

$$ \displaystyle\Tr\tilde{P}[\tilde{P},\Lambda_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}][M,[M,\tilde{\Lambda}_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}]] \displaystyle=\Tr(P_f \Lambda_{f \bq} \Lambda_{f -\bq} + \Lambda_{f -\bq} P_f \Lambda_{f \bq} - P_f \Lambda_{f \bq}P_f \Lambda_{f -\bq} - \Lambda_{f -\bq} P_f \Lambda_{f \bq} P_f)m^{\dagger}m \displaystyle-2\Tr P_{f}[P_{f},\Lambda_{f-{\boldsymbol{q}}}]m^{\dagger}\Lambda_{c-{\boldsymbol{q}}}m. $$

Finally we have

$$ 2\langle{\rm ad}_{\hat{M}}\rho_{\boldsymbol{q}}{\rm ad}_{\hat{M}}\rho_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}\rangle=2\langle\widehat{[M,\tilde{\Lambda}_{\boldsymbol{q}}]}\widehat{[M,\tilde{\Lambda}_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}]}\rangle=2\Tr\tilde{P}[M,\tilde{\Lambda}_{\boldsymbol{q}}][M,\tilde{\Lambda}_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}]-2\Tr\tilde{P}[M,\tilde{\Lambda}_{\boldsymbol{q}}]\tilde{P}[M,\tilde{\Lambda}_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}] $$

We evaluate each term by explicitly computing the commutators, splitting the trace into the two mirror sectors, and then eliminating dependence on $Q_{c}$ by using $m=-Q_{c}mQ_{f}$ . The first term is

$$ \displaystyle 2\Tr\tilde{P}[M,\tilde{\Lambda}_{\boldsymbol{q}}][M,\tilde{\Lambda}_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}] \displaystyle=2\Tr P_{c}(m\Lambda_{f{\boldsymbol{q}}}-\Lambda_{c{\boldsymbol{q}}}m)(m^{\dagger}\Lambda_{c-{\boldsymbol{q}}}-\Lambda_{f-{\boldsymbol{q}}}m^{\dagger}) \displaystyle+2\Tr P_{f}(m^{\dagger}\Lambda_{c{\boldsymbol{q}}}-\Lambda_{f{\boldsymbol{q}}}m^{\dagger})(m\Lambda_{f-{\boldsymbol{q}}}-\Lambda_{c-{\boldsymbol{q}}}m) \displaystyle=-2\Tr m^{\dagger}\Lambda_{c{\boldsymbol{q}}}\Lambda_{c-{\boldsymbol{q}}}m-2\Tr(P_f^\perp\Lambda_{f \bq} \Lambda_{f -\bq} + \Lambda_{f-\bq} P_f \Lambda_{f \bq})m^{\dagger}m \displaystyle+2\Tr(\Lambda_{f -\bq} m^\dag\Lambda_{c \bq} m + \Lambda_{f \bq} m^\dag\Lambda_{c -\bq} m), $$

and the second term is

$$ \displaystyle-2\Tr\tilde{P}[M,\tilde{\Lambda}_{\boldsymbol{q}}]\tilde{P}[M,\tilde{\Lambda}_{-{\boldsymbol{q}}}] \displaystyle=-2\Tr P_{c}(m\Lambda_{f{\boldsymbol{q}}}-\Lambda_{c{\boldsymbol{q}}}m)P_{f}(m^{\dagger}\Lambda_{c-{\boldsymbol{q}}}-\Lambda_{f-{\boldsymbol{q}}}m^{\dagger}) \displaystyle-2\Tr P_{f}(m^{\dagger}\Lambda_{c{\boldsymbol{q}}}-\Lambda_{f{\boldsymbol{q}}}m^{\dagger})P_{c}(m\Lambda_{f-{\boldsymbol{q}}}-\Lambda_{c-{\boldsymbol{q}}}m) \displaystyle=2\Tr(P_f^\perp\Lambda_{f \bq} P_f \Lambda_{f -\bq} + \Lambda_{f -\bq} P_f \Lambda_{f \bq} P_f^\perp)m^{\dagger}m. $$

We now collect terms from (S102), (S103), (S105), and (S106) and insert them back into (S100). First there is the term with two factors of $\Lambda_{c}$ in (S105); this is the TBG exchange energy

$$ \displaystyle-\frac{1}{4A}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{\rm eff}({\boldsymbol{q}})\left(-2\Tr m^{\dagger}\Lambda_{c{\boldsymbol{q}}}\Lambda_{c-{\boldsymbol{q}}}m\right)=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\bf p},{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{\rm eff}({\boldsymbol{q}})F_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\bf p})^{2}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}w^{\dagger}_{{\bf p}}w_{\bf p} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\bf p}2U_{\bf p}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}w^{\dagger}_{{\bf p}}w_{\bf p}, \displaystyle U_{\bf p} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\bf p},{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{\rm eff}({\boldsymbol{q}})F_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\bf p})^{2}, $$

where we used (S53), (S54). Next there are the terms with two factors of $\Lambda_{f}$ :

$$ \displaystyle\Tr(\Lambda_{f \bq} \Lambda_{f -\bq} P_f + \Lambda_{f -\bq} P_f \Lambda_{f \bq} - \Lambda_{f \bq}P_f \Lambda_{f -\bq} P_f - P_f \Lambda_{f -\bq} P_f \Lambda_{f \bq})m^{\dagger}m \displaystyle+\Tr(P_f \Lambda_{f \bq} \Lambda_{f -\bq} + \Lambda_{f -\bq} P_f \Lambda_{f \bq} - P_f \Lambda_{f \bq}P_f \Lambda_{f -\bq} - \Lambda_{f -\bq} P_f \Lambda_{f \bq} P_f)m^{\dagger}m \displaystyle-2\Tr(P_f^\perp\Lambda_{f \bq} \Lambda_{f -\bq} + \Lambda_{f-\bq} P_f \Lambda_{f \bq})m^{\dagger}m \displaystyle+2\Tr(P_f^\perp\Lambda_{f \bq} P_f \Lambda_{f -\bq} + \Lambda_{f -\bq} P_f \Lambda_{f \bq} P_f^\perp)m^{\dagger}m \displaystyle=\sum_{\bf p}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(2P_{f{\bf p}}-2P_{f{\bf p}}-P_{f{\bf p}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}P_{f{\bf p}}-P_{f{\bf p}}P_{f{\bf p}-{\boldsymbol{q}}}-P_{f{\bf p}}P_{f{\bf p}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}-P_{f{\bf p}-{\boldsymbol{q}}}P_{f{\bf p}}+2P_{f{\bf p}}^{\perp}P_{f{\bf p}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}+2P_{f{\bf p}-{\boldsymbol{q}}}P_{f{\bf p}}^{\perp})m^{\dagger}_{\bf p}m_{\bf p} \displaystyle=\sum_{\bf p}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(-\frac{1}{4}\{Q_{f{\bf p}},Q_{f{\bf p}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}+Q_{f{\bf p}-{\boldsymbol{q}}}\}-\frac{1}{2}Q_{f{\bf p}}Q_{f{\bf p}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}-\frac{1}{2}Q_{f{\bf p}-{\boldsymbol{q}}}Q_{f{\bf p}}\right)m^{\dagger}_{\bf p}m_{\bf p} $$

which gives the Dirac exchange energy,

$$ \displaystyle-\frac{1}{4A}\sum_{{\bf p},{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{\rm eff}({\boldsymbol{q}})\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(-\frac{1}{4}\{Q_{f{\bf p}},Q_{f{\bf p}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}+Q_{f{\bf p}-{\boldsymbol{q}}}\}-\frac{1}{2}Q_{f{\bf p}}Q_{f{\bf p}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}-\frac{1}{2}Q_{f{\bf p}-{\boldsymbol{q}}}Q_{f{\bf p}}\right)m^{\dagger}_{\bf p}m_{\bf p} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{{\bf p},{\boldsymbol{q}}}V_{\rm eff}({\boldsymbol{q}})\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\frac{1}{2}\{Q_{f{\bf p}},Q_{f{\bf p}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}\}m^{\dagger}_{\bf p}m_{\bf p} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\bf p}\mu}w^{*}_{{\bf p}\mu}(C\delta R^{D}C)^{\mu\nu}_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}w_{{\bf p}^{\prime}\nu} $$

where $\delta R^{D}$ is the renormalization to the dispersion energy $R^{D}\to R^{D}_{\rm eff}=R^{D}+\delta R^{D}$ due to the replacement $h^{\prime}_{D}\to h^{\prime D}_{\rm eff}=h^{\prime D}+\delta h^{\prime}_{D}$ with

$$ \delta h^{\prime}_{D}({\bf p})=\frac{1}{A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\rm eff}({\boldsymbol{q}})Q^{\prime}_{f}({\bf p}+{\boldsymbol{q}}),\qquad\delta R^{D}=\delta_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\{h^{\prime}_{D}({\bf p}),Q^{\prime}_{f}({\bf p}\}t^{\dagger}_{\mu}t_{\nu}. $$

At charge neutrality this renormalization is that of the Dirac velocity $v\to v_{\rm eff}=v+\delta v$ where

$$ \delta v\absolutevalue{\bp_+}=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\rm eff}({\boldsymbol{q}})\cos\left(\theta_{{\bf p}_{+}}-\theta_{{\bf p}_{+}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}\right). $$

is the usual velocity renormalization and $\theta_{{\boldsymbol{a}}}$ is the angle of a vector ${\boldsymbol{a}}$ .

Finally, there are the terms with one factor of $\Lambda_{c}$ and one factor of $\Lambda_{f}$ . They are

$$ \displaystyle-2\Tr[\Lambda_{f-{\boldsymbol{q}}},P_{f}]P_{f}m^{\dagger}\Lambda_{c{\boldsymbol{q}}}m-2\Tr P_{f}[P_{f},\Lambda_{f-{\boldsymbol{q}}}]m^{\dagger}\Lambda_{c-{\boldsymbol{q}}}m. \displaystyle+2\Tr(\Lambda_{f -\bq} m^\dag\Lambda_{c \bq} m + \Lambda_{f \bq} m^\dag\Lambda_{c -\bq} m) \displaystyle=2\sum_{\bf p}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(1-P_{f{\bf p}}+P_{f{\bf p}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}P_{f{\bf p}})m^{\dagger}_{{\bf p}}F_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\bf p})e^{i\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\bf p})}m_{{\bf p}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}+\text{c.c.} \displaystyle=2\sum_{\bf p}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(\frac{3}{4}+\frac{1}{4}Q_{f{\bf p}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}Q_{f{\bf p}}\right)m^{\dagger}_{{\bf p}}F_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\bf p})e^{i\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\bf p})\gamma_{z}}m_{{\bf p}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}+\text{c.c.} \displaystyle=2\sum_{\bf p}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Q_{f{\bf p}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}Q_{f{\bf p}}m^{\dagger}_{{\bf p}}F_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\bf p})e^{i\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\bf p})\gamma_{z}}m_{{\bf p}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}+\text{c.c.} \displaystyle=2\sum_{\bf p}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Q^{\prime}_{f{\bf p}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}Q^{\prime}_{f{\bf p}}w^{\dagger}_{{\bf p}}F_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\bf p})e^{i\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\bf p})\gamma_{z}}w_{{\bf p}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}+\text{c.c.} $$

where we used $Q_{c}m_{{\bf p}}Q_{f{\bf p}}=-m_{{\bf p}}$ to obtain the second to last line and the $C_{2}$ symmetry of the TBG form factors (S54) to obtain the last line.

Putting everything together and using the expansion (S92) we have

$$ E_{D}+E_{\rm int}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}\mu\nu}w^{*}_{\mu{\bf p}}\left(C_{\bf p}R_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}C_{{\bf p}^{\prime}}\right)^{\mu\nu}w_{\nu{\bf p}} $$

with

$$ \displaystyle R_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}^{\mu\nu} \displaystyle=R^{D\mu\nu}_{\text{eff}{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}+U_{\bf p}\delta_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}\delta^{\mu\nu}+\tilde{R}^{\mu\nu}_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}} \displaystyle\tilde{R}^{\mu\nu}_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}} \displaystyle=-\frac{1}{A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\rm eff}({\boldsymbol{q}})\delta_{{\bf p}+{\boldsymbol{q}},{\bf p}^{\prime}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Q^{\prime}_{f{\bf p}^{\prime}}Q^{\prime}_{f{\bf p}}t^{\mu{\dagger}}F_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\bf p})e^{i\phi_{{\boldsymbol{q}}}({\bf p})\gamma_{z}}t^{\nu}+\text{h.c.}. $$

#### SIV.1.3 Displacement and in plane field perturbations

Finally we evaluate the perturbation term (S85). It is nonzero at first order and acts as a source term:

$$ \displaystyle E_{\Xi} \displaystyle=-i\langle{\rm ad}_{\hat{M}}\hat{\Xi}\rangle=-i\langle\widehat{[M,\Xi]}\rangle=-i\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\tilde{P}[M,\Xi] \displaystyle=-i\Tr P_{c}(m\xi^{\dagger}-\xi m^{\dagger})-i\Tr P_{f}(m^{\dagger}\xi-\xi^{\dagger}m)=-i\Tr Q_{c}(m\xi^{\dagger}-\xi m^{\dagger}), $$

where in the final step we used $Q_{c}mQ_{f}=-m$ to relate the traces in each mirror sector. Using (S86) we obtain

$$ E_{\Xi}=-i\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}\mu}C^{\mu\nu}_{\bf p}w_{\nu{\bf p}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Q_{c}t_{\mu}\xi^{\prime{\dagger}}_{{\bf p}}-w^{*}_{\nu{\bf p}}C^{\nu\mu}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Q_{c}\xi^{\prime}_{\bf p}t^{{\dagger}}_{\mu}. $$

where $\xi_{\bf p}^{\prime}=\xi_{{\bf p},+}\eta_{+}+\xi_{-{\bf p},-}\eta_{-}$ .

#### SIV.1.4 Superexchange energy

We now have the effective energy functional

$$ E[w]=E_{D}+E_{\rm int}+E_{\Xi}=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}\mu\nu}w^{*}_{\mu{\bf p}}\left(C_{\bf p}R_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}C_{{\bf p}^{\prime}}\right)^{\mu\nu}w_{\nu{\bf p}}-i\sum_{{\bf p}\mu}C^{\mu\nu}_{\bf p}w_{\nu{\bf p}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Q_{c}t_{\mu}\xi^{\prime{\dagger}}_{\bf p}-w^{*}_{\nu{\bf p}}C^{\nu\mu}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Q_{c}\xi^{\prime}_{\bf p}t^{{\dagger}}_{\mu}. $$

Integrating out $w_{\mu{\bf p}}$ then gives

$$ E_{\rm SE}(Q_{c},Q_{f})=-2\sum_{{\bf p}\mu}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(Q_{c}t_{\mu}\xi^{\prime{\dagger}}_{\bf p}\right)\left(C_{\bf p}R^{-1}_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}C_{{\bf p}^{\prime}}\right)^{\mu\nu}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(Q_{c}\xi_{{\bf p}^{\prime}}t^{\dagger}_{\nu}\right). $$

Above we used that $C=C^{\dagger}=C^{2}$ is a projector. If we now decompose $t_{\nu}C^{\nu\mu}=\frac{1}{2}(t^{\mu}-Q_{c}t^{\mu}Q^{\prime}_{f{\bf p}})$ we obtain

$$ \displaystyle E_{\rm SE}(Q_{c},Q_{f})=-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}\mu\nu}\biggl( \displaystyle\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(Q_{c}t_{\mu}\xi^{\prime{\dagger}}_{\bf p}\right)R^{-1\mu\nu}_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(Q_{c}\xi^{\prime}_{{\bf p}^{\prime}}t^{{\dagger}}_{\nu}\right) \displaystyle-\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(t_{\mu}Q^{\prime}_{f{\bf p}}\xi^{\prime{\dagger}}_{\bf p}\right)R^{-1\mu\nu}_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(Q_{c}\xi^{\prime}_{{\bf p}^{\prime}}t^{{\dagger}}_{\nu}\right) \displaystyle-\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(Q_{c}t_{\mu}\xi^{\prime{\dagger}}_{\bf p}\right)R^{-1\mu\nu}_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(\xi^{\prime}_{{\bf p}^{\prime}}Q^{\prime}_{f{\bf p}}t^{{\dagger}}_{\nu}\right) \displaystyle+\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(t_{\mu}Q^{\prime}_{f{\bf p}}\xi^{\prime{\dagger}}_{\bf p}\right)R^{-1\mu\nu}_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(\xi^{\prime}_{{\bf p}^{\prime}}Q^{\prime}_{f{\bf p}}t^{{\dagger}}_{\nu}\right).\biggr). $$

An analytic evaluation of the above expression without further approximations is difficult because it is hard to invert $R$ . However, we may understand its essential features from a symmetry point of view.

First, we show that the above expression is $Q_{c}$ independent as long as $[Q_{c},\gamma_{z}]=0$ and $Q_{c}$ is approximately ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent near the ${\boldsymbol{K}}_{\eta}$ points. We first consider the first term which is quadratic in $Q_{c}$ . Note that $R$ , $\xi^{\prime}$ , and $Q_{f}^{\prime}$ have no dependence on pseudospin or real spin which implies $R$ is invariant under ${\rm U}(2n)$ basis rotations $t^{\mu}\mapsto Ut^{\mu}U^{\dagger}$ where $U\propto\gamma_{0}$ . Also, $[\xi^{\prime},U]=[Q_{f}^{\prime},U]=0$ , while this transformation induces $Q_{c}\mapsto U^{\dagger}Q_{c}U$ . A general ansatz for a quadratic in $Q_{c}$ term with $U(2n)$ invariance may be written as $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(Q_{c}\gamma_{\gamma})A^{\gamma\gamma^{\prime}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}(Q_{c}\gamma_{\gamma^{\prime}})$ , for some $2\times 2$ matrix $A$ . Here we used that $Q_{c}$ is diagonal in Chern sector to restrict Chern sector generators to the diagonal projectors $\gamma_{\gamma}$ . To restrict $A^{\gamma\gamma^{\prime}}$ , we note that $R$ is also invariant under $t^{\mu}\mapsto\gamma_{z}t^{\mu}$ . This transformation induces $Q_{c}\mapsto Q_{c}\gamma_{z}$ , which flips the sign of the off diagonal terms in $A$ . The diagonal terms of $A$ must be equal by $C_{2}\mathcal{T}$ symmetry, such that $A$ is proportional to the identity matrix the identity matrix and the term is independent of the choice of $Q_{c}$ . For the terms with one factor of $Q_{c}$ and one factor of $Q^{\prime}_{f}$ we also may use invariance under $C_{2}\mathcal{T}$ and ${\rm U}(2n)$ to show that if $Q^{\prime}_{f}$ preserves these symmetries then there may be no dependence on $Q_{c}$ except for a simple Hartree-like term $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Q_{c}$ when $\mu\neq 0$ .

However, mass terms and doping terms are arbitrarily low energy perturbations to the Dirac semimetal that may be generated in perturbation theory. Depending on the symmetry breaking of the TBG ground state, this may occur for the graphene electrons. Additionally, we may consider (S119) itself as a perturbation that acts as a dispersion term for the TBG electrons. We may do this numerically, but at charge neutrality we find very accurate and analytic results are obtainable if we neglect $\tilde{R}$ such that $R^{\mu\nu}_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}=2\delta_{{\bf p}{\bf p}^{\prime}}\delta^{\mu\nu}(v_{\rm eff}\absolutevalue{\bp_+}+U_{\bf p})$ . With this approximation we have

$$ \displaystyle E_{\rm SE}(Q_{c},Q_{f})=-\frac{1}{4}\sum_{{\bf p}\mu\nu}\frac{1}{v\absolutevalue{\bp_+}+U_{\bf p}}\biggl( \displaystyle\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(Q_{c}t_{\mu}\xi^{\prime{\dagger}}_{\bf p}\right)\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(Q_{c}\xi_{\bf p}t^{{\dagger}}_{\nu}\right) \displaystyle-\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(t_{\mu}Q^{\prime}_{f{\bf p}}\xi^{\prime{\dagger}}_{\bf p}\right)\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(Q_{c}\xi^{\prime}_{\bf p}t^{{\dagger}}_{\nu}\right) \displaystyle-\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(Q_{c}t_{\mu}\xi^{\prime{\dagger}}_{\bf p}\right)\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(\xi^{\prime}_{\bf p}Q^{\prime}_{f{\bf p}}t^{{\dagger}}_{\nu}\right) \displaystyle-\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(t_{\mu}Q^{\prime}_{f{\bf p}}\xi^{\prime{\dagger}}_{\bf p}\right)\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left(\xi^{\prime}_{\bf p}Q^{\prime}_{f{\bf p}}t^{{\dagger}}_{\nu}\right)\biggr). $$

We now use the Fierze identity for $t_{\mu}$ ,

$$ \mathop{\mathrm{tr}}At^{\mu}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Bt^{\mu{\dagger}}=\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}AB, $$

Applied to the superexchange energy, we obtain

$$ E_{\rm SE}(Q_{c},Q_{f})=-\frac{1}{4}\sum_{{\bf p}}\frac{1}{v\absolutevalue{\bp_+}+U_{\bf p}}(\text{const.}-2\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\xi^{\prime{\dagger}}_{\bf p}Q_{c}\xi^{\prime}_{\bf p}Q^{\prime}_{f{\bf p}}). $$

which is the result we obtain in the main text after undoing the ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to-{\boldsymbol{k}}$ transformation in valley $\eta=-1$ .

As discussed in the main text, the superexchange term also, indirectly, favors valley-diagonal TBG states since the energy can be lowered by developing a Dirac mass or valley dependent doping in this case. We show here that this energy is of order $V^{4}$ or $B^{4}$ when a Dirac mass is generated, for example the VH state, and of order $V^{6},B^{6}$ when a doping is generated. Let us consider the VH case with $Q_{c}=\eta_{z}\gamma_{z}$ ; a Chern insulator may be understood equivalently. The graphene sector has an effective dispersion

$$ h_{D}^{\rm{eff}}=h^{\prime}_{D}+m_{\bf p}\eta_{z}\gamma_{z},\qquad m_{\bf p}\approx\frac{m_{K}}{1+\frac{v\absolutevalue{\bp_+}}{U_{\bf p}}}, $$

which is minimized by $Q^{\prime}_{f}=-h_{D}^{\rm eff}/\sqrt{v^{2}k^{2}+m_{\bf p}^{2}}$ . Here $m_{K}=m_{\rm SE}\sim V^{2},B^{2}$ (29). Without loss of generality we take $m_{K}>0$ . Note that here we have ignored the ${\bf p}$ dependence of the matrix element $t_{{\bf p}++}$ and interaction energy $U_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ but kept the momentum dependence of the energy gap in the denominator; we will see that the mass is still important for momenta with $v\absolutevalue{\bp_+}\approx U_{K}\gg m_{K}$ but not for momenta with $v\absolutevalue{\bp_+}\approx vk_{\theta}$ which is the scale on which $t$ changes.

The energy of the VH state per unit cell, relative to an IVC state that does not see any superexchange, is lowered by

$$ \displaystyle E_{\rm VH}-E_{\rm IVC} \displaystyle=\frac{A_{M}}{A}\sum_{\bf p}\frac{1}{2}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}h_{D}^{\rm eff}Q^{\prime}_{f}-\frac{1}{2}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}h^{\prime}_{D}Q^{\prime(0)}_{f}=-2n\frac{A_{M}}{A}\sum_{\bf p}\left(\sqrt{v^{2}\absolutevalue{\bp_+}^{2}+m_{\bf p}^{2}}-v\absolutevalue{\bp_+}\right) \displaystyle=-2nA_{M}\int\frac{d^{2}p}{(2\pi)^{2}}\sqrt{v^{2}\absolutevalue{\bp_+}^{2}+m_{\bf p}^{2}}-v\absolutevalue{\bp}_{+} $$

Note that as we claimed above we may not approximate $m_{\bf p}=m_{K}$ ; if we do the integral becomes UV divergent. First we split the integral into the two regimes $x=v\absolutevalue{\bp_+}/m_{K}\ll\Lambda$ and $x\gg\Lambda$ with $1\ll\Lambda\ll x_{0}=U_{K}/m_{K}$ . In the former regime we can take $v\absolutevalue{\bp_+}\ll U_{K}$ and in the latter regime we may take $v\absolutevalue{\bp_+}\gg m_{K}$ .

$$ \displaystyle E_{\rm SE,\,VH}-E_{\rm SE,\,IVC} \displaystyle=-\frac{2nA_{M}m_{K}^{3}}{2\pi v^{2}}\int_{0}^{\Lambda}dx(x\sqrt{x^{2}+1}-x)+\int_{\Lambda}^{\infty}dx\left(x\sqrt{x^{2}+\frac{1}{(1+\frac{x}{x_{0}})^{2}}}-x^{2}\right) \displaystyle\approx-\frac{nA_{M}m_{K}^{3}}{2\pi v^{2}}\left(\int_{0}^{\Lambda^{2}}du(\sqrt{u+1}-\sqrt{u})+\int_{\Lambda}^{\infty}\frac{dx}{\left(1+\frac{x}{x_{0}}\right)^{2}}\right) \displaystyle\approx-\frac{nA_{M}m_{K}^{3}}{2\pi v^{2}}\left(\Lambda+\frac{1}{3}x_{0}-\Lambda\right) \displaystyle=-\frac{nA_{M}U_{K}m_{K}^{2}}{6\pi v^{2}}=-\frac{8\sqrt{3}n\pi U_{K}m_{K}^{2}}{54v^{2}k_{\theta}^{2}}. $$

The result is independent of the arbitrary intermediate scale $\Lambda$ we chose and as we claimed it is dominated by $x\approx x_{0}$ . The final result scales as $V^{4}$ because the energy gain is proportional to the square of the mass and as $(vk_{\theta})^{-2}$ because Dirac dispersion restricts the superexchange to a the vicinity of the $K_{M}$ point.

For a valley doping we have

$$ h_{D}^{\rm{eff}}=h^{\prime}_{D}+\mu_{\bf p}\eta_{z}. $$

We set $\mu_{\bf p}=\mu_{K}=m_{\rm SE}$ because we will see that only momenta with $v\absolutevalue{\bp_+}<\mu_{{\bf p}}$ contribute to the energy and for these momenta $\mu_{{\bf p}}\approx\mu_{K}$ . We also set $\mu_{K}>0$ without loss of generality. The energy is minimized by $Q^{\prime}=-h^{\prime}_{D}\Theta(v\absolutevalue{\bp_+}-\mu_{K})+\mathop{\mathrm{sgn}}\mu_{K}\Theta(\mu_{K}-v\absolutevalue{\bp_+})$ . We obtain for the energy per unit cell

$$ \displaystyle E_{\rm SE,\,VP}-E_{\rm SE,\,IVC} \displaystyle=\frac{A_{M}}{A}\sum_{\bf p}\frac{1}{2}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}h_{D}^{\rm eff}Q^{\prime}_{f}-\frac{1}{2}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}h^{\prime}_{D}Q^{\prime(0)}_{f}=-2n\frac{A_{M}}{A}\sum_{\bf p}(\mu-v\absolutevalue{\bp_+})\Theta(\mu-v\absolutevalue{\bp_+}) \displaystyle=\frac{-2nA_{M}}{2\pi}\int_{0}^{\mu/v}pdp(\mu-p)=\frac{nA_{M}\mu^{3}}{3\pi v^{2}}. $$

Notably, this energy is order $V^{6}$ and has little effect in our Hartree Fock simulations compared to the inter-Chern superexchange from the displacement field induced MATBG dispersion.

### SIV.2 Inter-TBG superexchange for $n=4$ and beyond

We now comment on how these results generalize to $n>3$ , in particular to the case when the superexchange occurs between two TBG subsystems. We assume one of the twisted bilayer graphene subsystems is at its magic angle and is strongly coupled near the ${\boldsymbol{K}}_{\pm}$ points and the others are sufficiently away from their magic angles that they may be approximated by their low energy Dirac cones. This approximation may break down if the screening from the various Dirac cones is strong enough to make the MATBG weakly coupled or if two magic angles are sufficiently close that the weak coupling approximation breaks for one of the nominally non-magic subsystems.

With this assumption, it is straightforward to generalize the trilayer graphene computation with only slight modifications. In particular, we no longer take ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to-{\boldsymbol{k}}$ in the negative graphene valley. This is because there is a potential for superexchange-induced IVC order in non-magic TBG subsystems since there are Dirac points in both valleys for each ${\boldsymbol{K}}_{\pm}$ point. Furthermore, this doubling of Dirac cones implies that the Dirac dispersion term $R^{D\mu\nu}\propto\delta^{\mu\nu}$ even without taking ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to-{\boldsymbol{k}}$ . When the MATBG has tunneling to a non-magic TBG as well as a graphene subsystem, the two superexchanges may be done separately and combined at the end. Alternatively, we may add a spectator graphene Dirac cone that is not tunneled into in order to perform the graphene superexchange computation without the ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to-{\boldsymbol{k}}$ transformation.

We now show the explicit results of this procedure for $n=4$ and $n=5$ . Consider $n=4$ with the BM Hamiltonian copied here for convenience,

$$ H^{\rm Full}_{\rm dec}=\left(\begin{array}[]{cccc}-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla-\lambda_{1}\Gamma_{+}&\varphi T({\boldsymbol{r}})&\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\Gamma_{+}&0\\
\varphi T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla+\lambda_{1}\Gamma_{-}&0&\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\Gamma_{-}\\
\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\Gamma_{+}&0&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla-\lambda_{2}\Gamma_{+}&\frac{1}{\varphi}T({\boldsymbol{r}})\\
0&\frac{2}{\sqrt{5}}\Gamma_{-}&\frac{1}{\varphi}T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla+\lambda_{2}\Gamma_{-}\end{array}\right). $$

For simplicity we work at charge neutrality, though there is no obstruction to introducing $\mu\neq 0$ in the same way we did for $n=3$ . We also neglect the off diagonal $\tilde{R}$ term and restrict the superexchange to the lowest energy BM bands of the non-magic TBG. We consider the first TBG to be magic. There is an external field driven superexchange with the second TBG. The second TBG has dispersion $h_{f}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ and occupations determined by $Q_{f}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ . Note that instead of working with ${\bf p}={\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{G}}$ here we work inside the first Brillouin zone since TBG doesn’t have continouous translation symmetry like graphene. The matrix $R$ for inter-TBG superexchange is essentially the same as the sandwich graphene $R$ : the maindifference is that the dispersion part $R^{D}$ is diagonal in $\mu,\nu$ indices without taking ${\boldsymbol{k}}\to-{\boldsymbol{k}}$ and is proportional to $\absolutevalue{h_f(\bk)}$ as opposed to $v\absolutevalue{\bp}$ .

The other difference involved in the inter-TBG superexchange is the matrix element $t_{{\boldsymbol{k}}\eta\gamma}=\bra{u_{c \bk\eta\gamma}}\ket{ u_{f \bk\eta\gamma} }$ is $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}$ symmetric; it contains no layer structure unlike the trilayer graphene matrix element which only involves the top layer of the magic sector. This symmetry ensures that the mass generated for the non-magic subsystem is the same for all $Q_{c}\propto\gamma_{z}$ . In particular the IVC mass will be the same as the VH mass, whereas there is no IVC mass in sandwich graphene.

In addition to the external fields lattice relaxation mixes the two MATBG sectors. Here we compute the superexchange associated with this effect. By redoing the mapping using the relaxed structure parameters, we find that the different values of $\kappa$ on the external interfaces versus the internal interfaces lead to the term

$$ \begin{pmatrix}0&-\tilde{w}_{0}U_{0}({\boldsymbol{r}})\\
\tilde{w}_{0}U_{0}(-{\boldsymbol{r}})&0\end{pmatrix} $$

in the lower left block of (S128) (and its hermitian conjugate in the upper right block). We find $\tilde{w}_{0}=3.27$ meV. This term is $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}$ asymmetric unlike the displacement field and therefore comes with an extra factor of $\eta$ in the projection $\xi_{\eta{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ . This doesn’t matter much, however, and this term will essentially act as an effective displacement field.

We now focus on five layers. We copy the BM Hamiltonian for five layers here for convenience:

$$ H^{\rm Full}_{\rm dec}=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccccc}-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&\sqrt{3}T({\boldsymbol{r}})&\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\Gamma_{+}&0&0\\
\sqrt{3}T^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{r}})&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{-}\cdot\nabla&0&\Gamma_{-}&0\\
\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}\Gamma_{+}&0&-iv_{F}{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}_{+}\cdot\nabla&T({\boldsymbol{r}})&\frac{4}{\sqrt{6}}\Gamma_{+}\\

First let us consider the first TBG, with tunneling amplitudes scaled by $\sqrt{3}$ , to be magic. Let us discuss the inter-TBG superexchange. The matrix elements

$$ \displaystyle t_{{\boldsymbol{k}}\eta\gamma} \displaystyle=\bra{u^*_{c \bk\eta\gamma}}\begin{pmatrix}\frac{2}{\sqrt{3}}&0\\
0&1\end{pmatrix}_{\rm Layer}\ket{u_{f \bk\eta\gamma'}} $$

are now neither $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}$ symmetric or $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}$ asymmetric either. As a result, the Dirac masses for $Q_{c}\propto\gamma_{z}\eta_{0,z}$ at the ${\boldsymbol{K}}_{\zeta}$ points in valley $\eta$ are different for $\zeta=\pm\eta$ . The $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}$ symmetric and $\mathcal{P}\mathcal{T}$ asymmetric parts of (S131) give rise to opposite masses for KIVC states that partially cancel out. Note, however, that the displacement field mixes the non-magic TBG with the graphene subsystem. We therefore expect the KIVC mass to not have a large impact. Similarly the valley diagonal masses will mostly be important near ${\boldsymbol{K}}_{-\eta}$ where there is no graphene Dirac cone.

When the second TBG subsector is at its magic angle external fields couple it to the non-magic TBG subsystem as well as the graphene subsystem, but the two non-magic subsystems do not couple to each other. In this case the masses will have more of an effect since they will not be dominated by mixing between the non-magic sectors. While lattice relaxation mixes the non-magic sectors, this will be overwhelmed once a large enough displacement field is applied.

## SV Weak coupling theory of pair-breaking

In this appendix, we provide details for the weak coupling theory of pair-breaking. We start by considering the band structure for adding electrons to the KIVC state at $\nu=2$ . First, we note that if we neglect the single-particle dispersion term, there is still dispersion generated due to interaction on top of the insulating ground state at any integer filling which is given exactly by the Hartree-Fock Hamiltonian [38, 119]. The insulating ground states at integer filling $\nu$ are described by $Q_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ which is ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ -independent and satisfies $\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}Q=2\nu$ and $[Q,\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})]=0$ for all ${\boldsymbol{k}}$ and ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ . The Hartree-Fock Hamiltonian for a state specified by the matrix $Q_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ is given by [28, 30]

$$ H_{\rm HF}[Q]({\boldsymbol{k}})=\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{G}}V_{\boldsymbol{G}}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{G}}({\boldsymbol{k}})\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\Lambda_{-{\boldsymbol{G}}}({\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime})Q_{\boldsymbol{k}}-\frac{1}{2A}\sum_{\boldsymbol{q}}V_{\boldsymbol{q}}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})Q_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}}\Lambda_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})^{\dagger} $$

We are interested in the vicinity of $\nu=2$ where we can take the ground state to be a spin-polarized KIVC state (other possibilities like spin-valley locked states are related to it by applying ${\rm U}(2)\times{\rm U}(2)$ rotations) [30]. The corresponding $Q$ can be taken to be $P_{\uparrow}\sigma_{0}\tau_{0}+P_{\downarrow}\sigma_{y}\tau_{y}$ [30], where $P_{\uparrow/\downarrow}$ denotes the projector onto the $\uparrow/\downarrow$ sector. Substituting in the Hartree-Fock Hamiltonian (S132) yields the dispersion shown in Fig. S3 [119]. We are going to focus on the case of electron doping where charge carriers enter the upper two bands which can be labelled by a band index $n=1,2$ . The effect of the in-plane field is obtained by projecting the term $\frac{g_{\text{orb}}}{2}\mu_{B}\mu_{z}\hat{z}\times{\bf B}\cdot{\boldsymbol{\sigma}}$ onto the KIVC bands:

$$ H_{\bf B}=\mu_{B}{\boldsymbol{g}}_{n,{\boldsymbol{k}}}\cdot{\bf B},\qquad{\boldsymbol{g}}_{n,{\boldsymbol{k}}}=\frac{g_{\text{orb}}}{2}\langle u_{n,{\boldsymbol{k}}}|\mu_{z}(\sigma_{y},-\sigma_{x}\tau_{z})|u_{n,{\boldsymbol{k}}}\rangle $$

The two components $g^{x,y}_{n,{\boldsymbol{k}}}$ for the two bands $n=1,2$ are plotted in Fig. S4.

In the following, we will restrict ourselves to intraband pairing and drop the band index $n$ . All the expressions that follow apply for either KIVC band $n=1,2$ . Given a KIVC band, we are going to assume there is some attractive interaction which gives rise to pairing in the KIVC bands and write the imaginary time Lagrangian

$$ \mathcal{L}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\dagger}[\partial_{\tau}+\xi_{\boldsymbol{k}}+\mu_{B}{\boldsymbol{g}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\bf B}]\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}-\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{q}}}v_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}({\boldsymbol{q}})\psi^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}/2}\psi^{\dagger}_{-{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}/2}\psi_{-{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}+{\boldsymbol{q}}/2}\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}+{\boldsymbol{q}}/2} $$

Here, $v_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}({\boldsymbol{q}})$ represents some attractive interaction such that $v_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}({\boldsymbol{q}})\geq 0$ . Note that the assumption of purely attractive interaction is not necessary here. It suffices to have some channel where the interaction is attractive, in which case we can understand $v_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}({\boldsymbol{q}})$ as the projection of the full interaction onto the attractive channels. In the following, we will not make any assumption about the origin of the attraction and will assume its effective for an energy range of $2\Lambda$ around the Fermi energy which will provide the cutoff for the momentum summation (note that we have ignored umklapp processes). $\xi_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ is the single particle KIVC energy spectrum.

To determine the effect of ${\bf B}$ on the superconducting $T_{c}$ , we will proceed in the standard fashion by introducing the Hubbard-Stratonovich field $\Delta_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{q}})$ leading to

$$ \mathcal{L}=\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\dagger}[\partial_{\tau}+\xi_{\boldsymbol{k}}+\mu_{B}{\boldsymbol{g}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\bf B}]\psi_{\boldsymbol{k}}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{q}}}[\Delta_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\dagger}({\boldsymbol{q}})\psi_{-{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}/2}\psi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}/2}+\Delta_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{q}})\psi^{\dagger}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}/2}\psi^{\dagger}_{-{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}/2}]+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{q}}}\Delta^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{q}})[v({\boldsymbol{q}})]^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}\Delta_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}({\boldsymbol{q}}) $$

The action at finite temperature is given by the standard expression $S=\int_{0}^{\beta}d\tau\mathcal{L}(\tau)$ . The order parameter field $\Delta_{\boldsymbol{q}}({\boldsymbol{k}})$ is generally assumed to be slowly varying in space (which means it is only non-zero for small ${\boldsymbol{q}}$ ) and time. Here, we will completely ignoring the $\tau$ dependence and introduce the Fourier transform for $\psi(\tau)$ in terms of Matsubara frequency

$$ \psi(\tau)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\beta}}\sum_{\omega_{n}}e^{i\omega_{n}\tau}\psi_{n},\qquad\omega_{n}=\frac{2n+1}{\beta}\pi $$

The action then becomes

$$ S=\frac{1}{2}\sum_{\omega_{n},{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{q}}}(\psi^{\dagger}_{n,{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}/2}\quad\psi_{-n,-{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}/2})\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}G^{-1}_{n,{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}/2}&\Delta^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{q}})\\
\Delta_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{q}})&-G^{-1}_{-n,-{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}/2}\end{array}\right)\left(\begin{array}[]{c}\psi_{n,{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}/2}\\
\psi^{\dagger}_{-n,-{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}/2}\end{array}\right)+\frac{\beta}{2}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{q}}}\Delta^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{q}})[v({\boldsymbol{q}})]^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}\Delta_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}({\boldsymbol{q}}) $$

where we introduced the single particle Green’s function

$$ G_{n,{\boldsymbol{k}}}=\frac{1}{i\omega_{n}+\xi_{\boldsymbol{k}}+\mu_{B}{\boldsymbol{g}}_{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\bf B}} $$

The fermions can be integrated out leading to a Pfafian which can be written in the exponential as the logarithm of the trace of some operator. The resulting free energy per unit cell can be expanded in powers of $\Delta$ as

$$ F=F_{0}+\frac{1}{2\beta N}\sum_{m,n,{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{q}}}\frac{1}{m}\mathop{\mathrm{tr}}\left[\left(\begin{array}[]{cc}0&G_{n,{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}/2}\Delta^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{q}})\\
-G_{-n,-{\boldsymbol{k}}+{\boldsymbol{q}}/2}\Delta_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{q}})&0\end{array}\right)\right]^{m}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime},{\boldsymbol{q}}}\Delta^{\dagger}_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{q}})[v({\boldsymbol{q}})]^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}\Delta_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}({\boldsymbol{q}}) $$

Taking the variation of $F$ relative to $\Delta_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{q}})$ gives the BCS self-consistency equation which incorporates the effect of the orbital field. Since we are interested in only identify $T_{c}$ for the different pairing channels and how it changes with in-plane field, we can make focus on the vicinity of $T=T_{c}$ where $\Delta$ is small small and restrict ourselves to the leading term in $\Delta^{\dagger}\Delta$ . In addition, we assume the order parameter $\Delta_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{q}})$ is spatially uniform which means that

$$ \Delta_{\boldsymbol{k}}({\boldsymbol{q}})=\delta_{{\boldsymbol{q}},0}\Delta_{\boldsymbol{k}} $$

Expanding to quadratic order in $\Delta$ , we get

$$ F=F_{0}+\frac{1}{2}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}\Delta_{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\dagger}\left\{[v(0)]^{-1}_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}-\frac{\delta_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}}{N}\Gamma_{\boldsymbol{k}}\right\}\Delta_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}},\qquad\Gamma_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{n}G_{n,{\boldsymbol{k}}}G_{-n,-{\boldsymbol{k}}} $$

$\Gamma_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ can be evaluated using the standard Matsubara summation trick

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma_{\boldsymbol{k}} \displaystyle=\frac{1}{\beta}\sum_{n}\frac{1}{(i\omega_{n}+\xi_{\boldsymbol{k}}+g_{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\bf B})(-i\omega_{n}+\xi_{\boldsymbol{k}}-\mu_{B}g_{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\bf B})}=\frac{\sinh\beta\xi_{\boldsymbol{k}}}{2\xi_{\boldsymbol{k}}(\cosh\beta\xi_{\boldsymbol{k}}+\cosh(\mu_B g_\bk\cdot\bB))} \displaystyle\simeq\frac{\tanh\frac{\beta\xi_{\boldsymbol{k}}}{2}}{2\xi_{\boldsymbol{k}}}-(\mu_{B}g_{\boldsymbol{k}}\cdot{\bf B})^{2}\frac{\beta^{2}\tanh\frac{\beta\xi_{\boldsymbol{k}}}{2}\sech^{2}\frac{\beta\xi_{\boldsymbol{k}}}{2}}{8\xi_{\boldsymbol{k}}} $$

The expression in (S141) can be written more compactly in the matrix form $\frac{1}{2}\hat{\Delta}^{\dagger}\left\{\hat{v}(0)^{-1}-\frac{1}{N}\hat{\Gamma}\right\}\hat{\Delta}$ where $\hat{\Delta}$ , $\hat{v}(0)$ , $\hat{\Gamma}$ are , respectively, an $N$ -component vector, an $N\times N$ matrix, and an $N\times N$ diagonal matrix in the momentum index. The different pairing channels correspond to the eigenvectors of $\hat{v}(0)^{-1}-\frac{1}{N}\hat{\Gamma}$ with the corresponding $T_{c}$ obtained as the value of $T$ for which the corresponding eigenvalue vanishes. This condition is equivalent to solving the linearized BCS equation which can be written compactly as

$$ \det\Xi(T_{c})=0,\qquad\hat{\Xi}(T)=\hat{1}-\frac{1}{N}\hat{v}(0)\hat{\Gamma}(T),\quad\leftrightarrow\quad\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}=\delta_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}-\frac{1}{N}[v(0)]_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}\Gamma_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}} $$

To simplify further, we make the standard assumption of the weak coupling theory that the relevant temperatures as well as the energy cutoff $\Lambda$ are much smaller than the Fermi energy. In this case, we can reduce the momentum integrals to integrals over the Fermi surface by writing

$$ \frac{1}{N}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\int\frac{d^{2}{\boldsymbol{k}}}{(2\pi)^{2}}=\int_{-\Lambda}^{\Lambda}d\xi N(\xi)\int\frac{d\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}}}{2\pi}=N(0)\int_{-\Lambda}^{\Lambda}d\xi\int\frac{d\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}}}{2\pi} $$

where $\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ is an angular variable labeling a point at the FS defined as $\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}}=\arg(k_{x}+ik_{y})$ , $N(\xi)$ is the density of states and $N(0)$ is the density of states at the Fermi energy. In the last equality, we used the assumption that the cutoff $\Lambda$ is much smaller than the Fermi energy such that the variations of the density of states for a window of $2\Lambda$ around the Fermi energy can be neglected.

We now make use of the rotation symmetry to express the matrix $\Xi$ in angular momentum basis. To make $C_{6}$ rotation symmetry manifest, we will write the angular momentum $l$ which is an integer as $m+6M$ where $m=-2,\dots,3$ and $M$ an integer. $C_{6}$ rotation symmetry implies the conservation of $l\mod 6=m$ . The angular momentum matrix elements are

$$ \displaystyle\langle m,M|\Xi|m^{\prime},M^{\prime}\rangle \displaystyle=\Xi_{m,m^{\prime};M,M^{\prime}}=\frac{1}{2\Lambda NN(0)}\sum_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}\Xi_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}e^{i(m+6M)\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}}-i(m^{\prime}+6M^{\prime})\phi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}} \displaystyle=\delta_{m,m^{\prime}}\delta_{M,M^{\prime}}-\sum_{M^{\prime\prime}}V_{m;M,M^{\prime\prime}}\Gamma_{m-m^{\prime},M^{\prime\prime}-M^{\prime}} $$

where $V_{m;M,M^{\prime}}$ and $\Gamma_{m;M}$ are defined as

$$ \Gamma_{m,M}=\frac{1}{N}\sum_{\boldsymbol{k}}\Gamma_{\boldsymbol{k}}e^{i(m+6M)\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}}}\qquad V_{m;M,M^{\prime}}=\int\frac{d\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}}}{2\pi}\int\frac{d\phi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}}{2\pi}[v(0)]_{{\boldsymbol{k}},{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}e^{i[m(\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}}-\phi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}})+6(M\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}}-M^{\prime}\phi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}})]} $$

Here, we used the rotation symmetry of $v[0]$ : $[v(0)]_{\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}}+\frac{2\pi}{6},\phi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}+\frac{2\pi}{6}}=[v(0)]_{\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}},\phi_{{\boldsymbol{k}}^{\prime}}}$ . Following the discussion in the main text, we can restrict ourselves to even angular momenta $m=0,\pm 2$ since these are the only possible pairing channels for a single Fermi surface with $\mathcal{T}^{\prime 2}=-1$ .

We now further assume that $V_{m;M,M^{\prime}}$ is only non-zero for $M=M^{\prime}=0$ : $V_{m;M,M^{\prime}}=\Delta_{M,0}\delta_{M^{\prime},0}V_{m}$ . This amounts to the assumption that the interaction does not change very rapidly as we go around the FS. Thus, in the following, we will drop the $M$ index. We note that time-reversal symmetry $\mathcal{T}^{\prime}$ implies $V_{-2}=V_{2}$ . The matrix $\Xi$ is now a $3$ matrix in the $m=0,\pm 2$ space given explicitly by

$$ \Xi=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1-V_{0}\Gamma_{0}&V_{0}\Gamma_{2}&V_{0}\Gamma_{-2}\\
V_{2}\Gamma_{2}&1-V_{2}\Gamma_{0}&V_{2}\Gamma_{4}\\
V_{2}\Gamma_{-2}&V_{2}\Gamma_{-4}&1-V_{2}\Gamma_{0}\end{array}\right) $$

Let us start by considering the case of zero field first. Since the Fermi energy is approximately circular, we can take $\xi_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ to be only a function of $|{\boldsymbol{k}}|$ . At zero field, this leads to the simplification

$$ \Gamma_{m}=\delta_{m,0}N(0)\int_{-\Lambda}^{\Lambda}d\xi\frac{\tanh\frac{\beta\xi}{2}}{2\xi}=\delta_{m,0}N(0)\log\beta\tilde{\Lambda},\qquad\tilde{\Lambda}=\frac{2e^{\gamma_{E}}}{\pi}\Lambda $$

where $\gamma_{E}\approx 0.577$ is the Euler constant.

Thus, the eigenvalues of $\Xi$ are given by

$$ \lambda_{m}=1-V_{m}N(0)\log\beta\tilde{\Lambda},\quad\implies\quad T_{m}=\tilde{\Lambda}e^{-\frac{1}{N(0)V_{m}}} $$

This yields the famous BCS expression $T_{c}=\tilde{\Lambda}e^{-\frac{1}{N(0){\rm max}(V_{2},V_{0})}}$ .

For non-zero magnetic field, $\Gamma_{m}({\bf B})$ , we start by introducing the notation $B=|{\bf B}|e^{i\arg(B_{x}+iB_{y})}$ and $g_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}=|{\boldsymbol{g}}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}|e^{i\arg(g^{x}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}+ig^{y}_{{\boldsymbol{k}}})}$ leading to

$$ \displaystyle\Gamma_{m}({\bf B})=\delta_{m,0}N(0)\log\beta\tilde{\Lambda}-\frac{1}{4}c\beta^{2}N(0)\mu_{B}^{2}(B^{2}\bar{\chi}_{-m}+\bar{B}^{2}\chi_{m}+2B\bar{B}\gamma_{m}), \displaystyle c=\int dx\frac{\tanh\frac{x}{2}\sech^{2}\frac{x}{2}}{8x}=-7\zeta^{\prime}(-2)\approx 0.21314,\qquad\gamma_{m}=\int\frac{d\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}}}{2\pi}|g_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}|^{2}e^{im\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}}},\qquad\chi_{m}=\int\frac{d\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}}}{2\pi}g_{{\boldsymbol{k}}}^{2}e^{im\phi_{\boldsymbol{k}}} $$

We now note that $g_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ transforms under $C_{6}$ rotations as $g_{C_{6}{\boldsymbol{k}}}=e^{\frac{2\pi i}{6}}g_{\boldsymbol{k}}$ (cf. Fig. S4). This implies that $\gamma_{m}=0$ unless $m=0\mod 6$ and $\chi_{m}=0$ unless $m=-2\mod 6$ . Substituting in (S147) yields

$$ \Xi=\left(\begin{array}[]{ccc}1-V_{0}N(0)[\log\beta\tilde{\Lambda}-\frac{1}{2}c\beta^{2}\mu_{B}^{2}|B|^{2}\gamma_{0}]&-\frac{1}{4}c\beta^{2}V_{0}N(0)\mu_{B}^{2}B^{2}\bar{\chi}_{-2}&-\frac{1}{4}c\beta^{2}V_{0}N(0)\mu_{B}^{2}\bar{B}^{2}\chi_{-2}\\
-\frac{1}{4}c\beta^{2}V_{2}N(0)\mu_{B}^{2}B^{2}\bar{\chi}_{-2}&1-V_{2}N(0)[\log\beta\tilde{\Lambda}-\frac{1}{2}c\beta^{2}\mu_{B}^{2}|B|^{2}\gamma_{0}]&0\\
-\frac{1}{4}c\beta^{2}V_{2}N(0)\mu_{B}^{2}\bar{B}^{2}\chi_{-2}&0&1-V_{2}N(0)[\log\beta\tilde{\Lambda}-\frac{1}{2}c\beta^{2}\mu_{B}^{2}|B|^{2}\gamma_{0}]\end{array}\right) $$

The leading correction to the eigenvalues $\lambda_{m}$ of $\Xi$ can be obtained perturbatively. Notice that the off-diagonal terms will only affect the eigenvalues to order ${\bf B}^{4}$ unless the diagonal terms are degenerate i.e. $V_{0}\approx V_{2}$ which can only be realized through fine tuning since these channels are not related by any symmetry. Thus, assuming we can neglect the off-diagonal terms, we find that the eigenvalues of $\Xi$ are given by

$$ \lambda_{m}=1-V_{m}N(0)[\log\beta\tilde{\Lambda}-\frac{1}{2}c\beta^{2}\mu_{B}^{2}\gamma_{0}{\bf B}^{2}]+O({\bf B}^{4})\quad\implies\quad T_{m}({\bf B})=T_{m}[1-\frac{c\mu_{B}^{2}\gamma_{0}}{T_{m}^{2}}{\bf B}^{2}]+O({\bf B}^{4}) $$

Thus, we get the expression for the $T_{c}$ as a function of field

$$ \frac{T_{c}({\bf B})}{T_{c}}=1-\frac{c\mu_{B}^{2}\gamma_{0}}{2T_{c}^{2}}{\bf B}^{2} $$

Rather remarkabely, this expression does not depend explicitly on the pairing channel. This can be solved for the critical field:

$$ \frac{B_{c}}{T_{c}}=\frac{2}{\mu_{B}\sqrt{c\gamma_{0}}} $$

We can use this relation to relate the critical field due to in-plane orbital effect to the Pauli field given by $B_{p}=[1.86T/K]T_{c}$ . This leads to the simple relation between the orbital in-plane critical field and the Pauli field

$$ \frac{B_{c}}{B_{p}}=3.5\frac{1}{\sqrt{\gamma_{0}}}. $$
